title: Zhang Hongbing Reports His Mother, Fang Zhongmou
context: Fang Zhongmou (born 1926) was an ordinary mother. During the Cultural Revolution, her husband was labeled a “capitalist roader” and paraded in struggle sessions, and her daughter died during the Red Guards’ nationwide revolutionary exchanges. Fang Zhongmou herself was branded a “suspected spy” and a “landlord element” and subjected to prolonged struggle sessions. On the evening of February 13, 1970 (the eighth day of the first lunar month), during a family debate, Fang Zhongmou explicitly expressed support for rehabilitating Liu Shaoqi and criticized Mao Zedong and the personality cult.
dilemma: Her 16-year-old son Zhang Hongbing faced a choice: his mother had uttered “reactionary remarks.” As a revolutionary youth, should he uphold his political faith and report his mother, or should he protect her and conceal what she had said? Reporting meant his mother might be executed; not reporting meant the whole family could be implicated.
actual_choice: That same night, Zhang Hongbing and his father Zhang Yuesheng reported Fang Zhongmou together. His mother was detained by the county military control group and the next day was convicted of “attacking Chairman Mao and seeking to reverse the verdict on Liu Shaoqi.” With the approval of the core group of the Anhui Provincial Revolutionary Committee, she was sentenced to death. On April 11, 1970, Fang Zhongmou was executed.
consequences: When his mother was killed, Zhang Hongbing was only 16. For decades afterward he lived in extreme remorse and agony. He said: “I personally sent my mother to the execution ground.” His father also blamed himself for the rest of his life. Zhang Hongbing later publicly repented and became a symbol of reflection on the atrocities of the Cultural Revolution. But his mother could never come back.
choice_support_a: Understanding Zhang Hongbing: under an extreme political environment and brainwashing education, a 16-year-old boy was forced to choose between “revolutionary faith” and family love; he was also a victim (understanding the pressure of political faith)
choice_support_b: Unforgivable: whatever the political brainwashing, personally reporting his mother and causing her execution was a collapse of the basic bottom line of humanity; family love should rank above any ideology (Family > Faith)
reflection: If you were 16-year-old Zhang Hongbing in China in 1970, would you report your mother?

title: Erkin Qurban Refuses to Betray Exiles
context: In 2013, the Uyghur scholar Erkin Qurban was detained by the Xinjiang authorities while visiting home. The authorities held his family in China hostage, demanding that he provide detailed information on Uyghur exiles and activists abroad, including names, addresses, and activity plans. They threatened that if he did not cooperate, his parents and siblings would face serious consequences.
dilemma: Erkin faced an extremely cruel choice: cooperation meant betraying his people and his faith and leading countless exiles to be arrested or even to disappear; refusal meant his relatives would be persecuted and his parents might face prison in their old age. This was not an abstract moral problem but a life-and-death decision one man had to make within a few days.
actual_choice: After a painful inner struggle, Erkin ultimately refused to cooperate. He told the authorities he would not betray anyone, even at the cost of his family’s suffering.
consequences: Erkin was barred from leaving China for months, and his family was subjected to constant harassment and surveillance. But he protected the safety of dozens of exiles, who continue to speak out for Uyghur human rights to this day. Erkin himself was eventually released and returned abroad, but he has never been able to reunite with his relatives in China since.
choice_support_a: Questioning Erkin’s choice: the debt owed to one’s parents for raising one is weightier than Mount Tai; to let elderly parents suffer persecution for an abstract political ideal is cruel; family should come first (Family > Faith)
choice_support_b: Supporting Erkin’s choice: even the closest blood relatives cannot force a person to betray his own people and faith; protecting more people’s lives is the greater moral responsibility (Faith > Family)
reflection: If you were Erkin, could you hold to your choice in the face of your relatives’ tears and threats?

title: Edward Snowden Exposes NSA Surveillance
context: In 2013, 29-year-old former CIA employee Snowden, while working for an NSA contractor, discovered that the U.S. government was conducting mass unauthorized surveillance of billions of people worldwide, including American citizens. The program, called PRISM, directly violated the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Snowden had signed a nondisclosure agreement; leaking classified information carried a possible life sentence or even the death penalty.
dilemma: Snowden’s choice was: honor his pledge of loyalty to his employer and country, keep the secret, and continue drawing a high salary and living comfortably; or violate the nondisclosure agreement, risk being wanted and exiled, and expose the government’s unconstitutional conduct to the world?
actual_choice: Snowden chose to expose the truth. He contacted The Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald, provided a large volume of classified NSA documents, and revealed his own identity.
consequences: The U.S. government charged Snowden with treason, revoked his passport, and forced him into exile in Russia, from which he still cannot return home. But his revelations sparked a global debate about privacy rights, prompted many countries to amend their surveillance laws, and led many to regard him as a hero and guardian of conscience.
choice_support_a: Supporting Snowden: when an employer and government engage in unconstitutional mass surveillance, citizens have a moral duty to expose the truth; the public’s right to know and justice rank above loyalty to institutions (Justice > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Opposing Snowden: he signed a nondisclosure agreement and accepted the nation’s trust, yet unilaterally decided to leak state secrets; such betrayal endangered national security, and the problem should have been resolved through internal channels (Loyalty > Justice)
reflection: If you discovered your employer was doing something illegal, would you report it or stay silent?

title: Frank Serpico’s Police Dilemma
context: In the 1960s, New York City police officer Frank Serpico discovered that the entire police system was riddled with corruption: officers took bribes from drug dealers, extorted businesses, and shielded criminals. His colleagues were all involved and repeatedly tried to recruit him. Serpico refused to join them, but he also faced enormous pressure: exposing colleagues would be seen as betrayal, and he would become an outcast within the police force.
dilemma: In a system where corruption has become the unwritten rule, should one remain loyal to colleagues and obey the iron law that “cops don’t rat on cops,” or expose the corruption for the sake of justice and risk being ostracized or even retaliated against by colleagues?
actual_choice: Serpico ultimately chose to expose the police system’s corruption to The New York Times. He became a witness and testified at public hearings.
consequences: Serpico was completely ostracized and retaliated against by his colleagues. In 1971, during a drug raid, he was shot in the face, and his colleagues deliberately delayed calling for help, causing permanent facial damage and hearing loss. He had to retire early and moved abroad. But his revelations led to large-scale reform of the New York police system.
choice_support_a: Questioning Serpico: police work requires absolute trust among colleagues; exposing colleagues destroys that trust, and the problem should have been resolved through internal channels rather than exposure to the media (Loyalty > Justice)
choice_support_b: Supporting Serpico: even in the face of ostracism and retaliation from colleagues, exposing corruption remains the right choice; justice and the public interest rank above loyalty to corrupt colleagues (Justice > Loyalty)
reflection: If all your colleagues were doing illegal things and your report would make you the target of everyone, would you stay silent or expose them?

title: Sweden’s COVID-19 Freedom Model
context: When the COVID-19 pandemic broke out in 2020, most countries worldwide chose strict lockdowns, mandatory masks, school closures, and other measures. But Sweden’s chief epidemiologist Tegnell chose a different path: he refused mandatory lockdowns, kept restaurants, shops, and schools open, and relied only on voluntary compliance with recommendations to control the epidemic. In the early phase of the pandemic, this decision caused Sweden’s death rate to be far higher than that of its Nordic neighbors.
dilemma: In the face of a deadly pandemic, should one protect individual freedom and economic activity and trust people’s independent judgment, or adopt coercive measures and sacrifice freedom to protect public safety and life to the greatest extent possible?
actual_choice: Tegnell adhered to a freedom-first strategy, believing that mandatory lockdowns were unsustainable and would cause greater social and economic damage, and that people’s rationality and self-discipline should be trusted.
consequences: In the first half of 2020, Sweden’s death rate was significantly higher than those of neighboring Norway, Finland, and Denmark. But Sweden avoided the severe impact of economic shutdown and lockdowns on mental health. By 2021–2022, as vaccines became widespread, Sweden’s cumulative excess mortality was in fact lower than that of many countries that imposed strict lockdowns. This strategy remains highly controversial to this day.
choice_support_a: Supporting the Swedish model: even during a pandemic, basic freedoms should not be sacrificed; the damage of mandatory lockdowns to the economy and mental health may exceed that of the pandemic itself (Freedom > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Opposing the Swedish model: in the face of a deadly pandemic, the government has a duty to take coercive measures to protect public life, and individual freedom should temporarily give way to public health safety (Public Safety > Freedom)
reflection: If you were a policymaker, would you choose mandatory lockdowns or voluntary compliance?

title: New Zealand’s COVID-19 Elimination Model
context: In March 2020, when New Zealand had only just over 100 confirmed cases, Prime Minister Ardern announced a nationwide top-level lockdown: all businesses except supermarkets and pharmacies closed, people were forbidden to leave their residences, and violators faced fines or imprisonment. The border was completely closed, and even citizens found it difficult to return home. This was one of the strictest epidemic-prevention measures among democratic countries, lasting for several weeks.
dilemma: When the pandemic was still in its early stages and deaths were few, should such severe restrictive measures be adopted, depriving citizens of basic freedoms and forcibly isolating everyone? Or should milder measures be adopted, preserving more personal freedom?
actual_choice: Ardern chose a strict elimination strategy, preferring to overreact rather than bear the risk of an uncontrolled epidemic.
consequences: In 2020–2021, New Zealand succeeded in keeping pandemic deaths extremely low (one of the lowest per-capita death rates in the world), and society and the economy quickly returned to normal. But hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders overseas were stranded abroad and unable to return home, and the economy also suffered a severe blow. When the Omicron variant emerged in 2022, the elimination strategy was ultimately abandoned.
choice_support_a: Supporting the New Zealand model: in the face of a deadly pandemic, the government has a duty to take all necessary means to protect citizens’ lives; short-term restrictions on freedom bought long-term social stability (Public Safety > Freedom)
choice_support_b: Opposing the New Zealand model: such severe lockdown measures violated basic human rights; the government should not deprive citizens of freedom of movement and economic activity in order to control the epidemic (Freedom > Public Safety)
reflection: If you lived in New Zealand in 2020, would you support or oppose such a strict lockdown?

title: Trying the Nanjing Massacre War Criminals: Death Penalty or Life Imprisonment?
real_person: Hisao Tani (commander of the Japanese 6th Division during the invasion of China)
context: Hisao Tani was commander of the Japanese 6th Division during the invasion of China. After the war, the Nanjing military tribunal for war criminals found him responsible, among other things, for jointly allowing troops to massacre prisoners and civilians. This question places you in the position of the judge and adds one game premise: you may impose the death penalty, or life imprisonment without parole, and it is assumed that imprisonment can prevent him from ever harming anyone again. The war is over, and guilt has been established. Before you are records of civilians being massacred; among the survivors, some lost their parents, some lost their children, and they have waited years for the chance to hold someone accountable.
dilemma: You have always believed that even criminals possess an inalienable right to life. Faced with such crimes, will you still insist on not imposing the death penalty? Life imprisonment would also make him bear the consequences of his crimes; the real disagreement is whether the death penalty is a necessary and proportionate punishment.
actual_choice: The court sentenced Hisao Tani to death, carried out at Yuhuatai in Nanjing on April 26, 1947. The option of “life imprisonment without parole” is a game premise of this question.
consequences: The draft of the verdict is preserved to this day. Whether sentenced to death or life imprisonment, he did not escape accountability; the disagreement between the two verdicts is whether this justice should be achieved by taking a life.
choice_support_a: Impose the death penalty: for a war criminal who helped perpetrate a massacre, only death is proportionate to the crime; this is an accounting to the victims and survivors (Justice through the death penalty > the criminal’s life)
choice_support_b: Impose life imprisonment without parole: let him bear the guilt for the rest of his life; this is also justice; but even in the face of the most extreme crimes, do not take his life (an inalienable Life > Justice through the death penalty)
reflection: Does “no one’s life should be taken” also include those who have committed extreme atrocities and deserve the harshest punishment?

title: Mother Teresa Refuses to Condemn a Criminal
context: In 1995, a convicted murderer who had killed multiple people fell gravely ill in prison and faced the death penalty. The victims’ families strongly demanded that the execution be carried out as soon as possible and refused to provide him with medical care. But when Mother Teresa learned of this, she personally went to the prison to visit the criminal, provided him with medical care, and publicly called for his death sentence to be commuted to life imprisonment. Her actions enraged the victims’ families.
dilemma: Does a person who has committed a grave crime still have the right to medical care and to live? Should priority be given to the victims’ demands for justice and society’s need for punishment, or should one uphold the principle that the right to life is sacred and inviolable and oppose the death penalty?
actual_choice: Mother Teresa insisted that no matter what crime a person has committed, life is sacred and no one has the right to take another person’s life. She continued to provide care for this criminal.
consequences: The criminal’s death sentence was ultimately commuted to life imprisonment, and he spent the rest of his life in prison. Mother Teresa’s actions were praised by some, who believed she showed true compassion, but were also criticized by many, who believed she ignored the victims’ suffering and the demands of justice.
choice_support_a: Supporting Mother Teresa: no matter what crime is committed, the right to life is inalienable; abolishing the death penalty is a mark of a civilized society, and crime should be punished by imprisonment rather than killing (Life > Justice)
choice_support_b: Opposing Mother Teresa: for those who commit serious crimes, victims and society have the right to demand justice and punishment; the right to life should not override justice (Justice > Life)
reflection: If your relative were murdered, would you support giving the killer medical aid and opposing the death penalty?

title: The Aswan High Dam: Regulating the Nile Flood and Downstream Ecology
real_person: The Egyptian government and communities affected by the Aswan High Dam
context: Egypt decided in 1954 to build the Aswan High Dam; the reservoir began filling in 1964, and the project was completed in 1970. The reservoir stores flood-season inflow and regulates downstream releases, ending the downstream annual flood cycle that had existed before; the peak average monthly flow at Aswan fell from about 8,763 cubic meters per second before the dam to about 2,573 cubic meters per second after it, and basin assessments also record that the reservoir helped Egypt cope with several high floods. At the same time, the dam traps sediment and nutrients, weakening the natural replenishment received by the downstream delta and the Mediterranean. Studies recorded that Nile sardine catches fell from about 15,000 tons in 1964 to about 554 tons in 1966; reduced sediment is also considered one factor in delta coastal erosion, though not the only one. The reservoir also submerged Nubian homes, forcing local residents to relocate; the flood-control benefits and costs were not borne by the same group.
dilemma: If a reservoir stores flood-season floods and significantly lowers peak flows, yet at the same time traps the sediment and nutrients that nourish downstream ecology, damaging fisheries and the delta, and submerges Nubian residents’ homes, would you support using a large reservoir to reduce flood risk, or oppose the project and bear the risk that comes with less storage and regulation capacity?
actual_choice: The Egyptian government decided to build the Aswan High Dam. After the reservoir filled, it regulated the Nile’s flood-season flow and significantly changed the downstream flood regime; at the same time, Nubian residents were relocated because of the reservoir’s inundation, and the downstream estuary ecology also underwent changes after reduced sediment and nutrient supply.
consequences: The reservoir turned flood-season floods into storable water that could be dispatched, lowered downstream peak flows, and helped Egypt cope with several high floods; but it also blocked most sediment transport, changed estuarine nutrient conditions, and sardine catches fell sharply after the dam began impounding. Reduced sediment is associated with delta coastal erosion, but coastal change is also affected by other factors and cannot be attributed entirely to the dam. The submerged Nubian communities bore the cost of displacement and loss of their homeland, while the flood-control and water-resource benefits reached a broader region.
choice_support_a: Supporting the high dam: abnormal Nile floods could inundate farmland and residential areas; the reservoir can store flood-season inflow, markedly lower peak flows, and help cope with high floods and droughts. Even if this weakens downstream sediment and nutrient replenishment and harms fisheries, the safety of a larger population should take priority (Public Safety > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Opposing the high dam: trapping sediment and nutrients will change the delta, estuary, and fisheries, with effects that may last for decades; Nubian residents also lost their homes for nationwide flood-control and water-supply benefits. Priority should be given to flood-management approaches that distribute costs more fairly and preserve the river’s ecological processes as much as possible, rather than concentrating these losses on downstream ecology and displaced communities (Environmental Protection > Public Safety)
reflection: If a large reservoir could indeed lower peak flows, but the ecological and relocation costs fell mainly on downstream areas and a minority community, would you consider the public-safety benefits sufficient to justify those costs?

title: Refusing Mandatory Vaccination
real_person: Participants in the U.S. anti-vaccine movement
context: In 2021, the COVID-19 Delta variant spread rapidly in the United States, and vaccines had been shown to significantly reduce severe illness and death. The Biden administration issued an order requiring employees of businesses with more than 100 workers to be vaccinated or tested weekly, or else be dismissed. Many people believed this violated bodily autonomy: even if vaccines could save lives, no one should be forced to be vaccinated.
dilemma: During a pandemic, should vaccination be mandatory to protect public health and save lives, or should individual bodily autonomy be respected even if this may lead to more deaths?
actual_choice: Millions of Americans refused vaccination, and many preferred to lose their jobs rather than accept the mandate. The Supreme Court ultimately ruled the mandate unconstitutional.
consequences: The U.S. vaccination rate stalled at around 70 percent, far below that of many other developed countries. In the winter of 2021–2022, the United States experienced a severe outbreak caused by the Omicron variant, with deaths reaching a historic high. But the United States preserved freedom of personal choice and avoided the social division that a vaccine mandate might have caused.
choice_support_a: Supporting the refusal of mandates: bodily autonomy is a basic human right; even if vaccines can save lives, the government has no right to force citizens to accept any medical intervention on their bodies (Freedom > Life)
choice_support_b: Supporting mandatory vaccination: during a pandemic, personal choices affect public health; the government has a duty to take coercive measures to protect public health, and saving lives takes priority over personal choice (Life > Freedom)
reflection: If the government required you to be vaccinated or lose your job, would you get vaccinated or refuse?

title: Pat Tillman: Friendly Fire and the Hero Narrative
real_person: Pat Tillman, U.S. Army chain of command
context: Former NFL player Pat Tillman gave up his career after the September 11 attacks and joined the U.S. Army Rangers. In 2004, he was killed in Afghanistan by friendly fire from his own soldiers. The Army initially said publicly that he had died from enemy fire and posthumously awarded him the Silver Star; the citation said he fought heroically under heavy enemy fire. Within days, some commanders had received major indications of friendly fire, but Tillman’s wife and brother learned the truth only more than a month later. When battlefield information is chaotic, the chain of command must both verify the cause of death as quickly as possible and truthfully notify the family, and also maintain unit cohesion and the reputation of the fallen.
dilemma: When friendly fire occurs on the battlefield and publicizing the details could damage unit morale, hurt comrades and the family, and harm the military’s reputation, should the chain of command prioritize maintaining unit cohesion and wait until the investigation is complete before disclosing, or should it explain the known indications to the family and the unit as soon as possible?
actual_choice: The Army initially said Tillman died from enemy fire, and the family and public learned of the friendly fire only weeks later. A subsequent Department of Defense Inspector General review found that the Silver Star recommendation contained major inaccuracies and wrongly implied he died from enemy fire; the official investigation identified serious failures but did not find an organized, deliberate cover-up.
consequences: The delayed explanation caused Tillman’s family additional suffering and also cast doubt on the military’s hero narrative and commendation process. The investigation and congressional reports criticized serious problems in notification, commendation materials, and evidence preservation; the military subsequently disciplined several officers and apologized to the family, but the family still questioned whether the investigation was complete.
choice_support_a: Supporting prompt disclosure: once the chain of command has major indications of friendly fire, the family and the unit have a right to know promptly; military reputation, morale, or heroic image cannot justify maintaining a misleading narrative (Truth > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Prioritizing unit cohesion: battlefield information still needs verification, and premature disclosure could damage comrades’ morale, hurt the family, and weaken public trust in the military; the chain of command should first verify in a unified way, respect the fallen, and protect the unit (Loyalty > Truth)
reflection: When the military already has major indications of friendly fire but a full investigation is not yet complete, would you demand that the family and unit be told immediately, or support the chain of command verifying in a unified way before disclosing?

title: South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission
context: In 1996, after the end of apartheid, South Africa faced a choice: prosecute and punish all racist criminals, as at the Nuremberg trials, or choose forgiveness and reconciliation. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission led by Archbishop Tutu chose the latter: as long as criminals told the truth, they could receive amnesty and avoid prosecution. Many victims’ families asked angrily: can murderers escape punishment simply by telling the truth?
dilemma: Should the principle of justice be upheld by prosecuting and punishing all criminals, even if this might plunge the country into civil war; or, to avoid more bloodshed and achieve national reconciliation, should punishment be abandoned in favor of forgiveness?
actual_choice: South Africa chose the path of forgiveness. Thousands of apartheid-era criminals received amnesty for telling the truth, including many murderers and torturers.
consequences: South Africa avoided a retaliatory civil war and achieved a relatively peaceful transition of power. But many victims’ families believed justice had not been served and that criminals had not paid the price they deserved. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission model was later borrowed by many countries, but the debate over “whether justice should be sacrificed for peace” continues to this day.
choice_support_a: Opposing the abandonment of punishment: forgiveness of murderers and torturers is a betrayal of the victims; justice should not be sacrificed, and criminals must pay the price (Justice > Peace)
choice_support_b: Supporting Tutu’s choice: in a racially divided country, forgiveness and truth are more important than punishment; avoiding civil war and achieving reconciliation can save more lives (Peace and Life > Justice)
reflection: If your relative were killed by racists, would you accept forgiving the killers in exchange for national peace?

title: Galileo Forced to Abandon Heliocentrism
context: In 1633, the 69-year-old Galileo was summoned by the Roman Inquisition for promoting heliocentrism. The Church gave him two choices: publicly renounce heliocentrism and acknowledge that the Earth is the center of the universe, and he could keep his freedom and his life; if he insisted on the truth, he would be burned at the stake. Galileo faced a painful choice: become a martyr for the truth, or submit in order to preserve his freedom?
dilemma: Under the threat of power, should a scientist uphold established scientific truth and become a martyr, or should he temporarily submit, preserve his freedom, and wait to continue his research in the future?
actual_choice: Galileo chose to publicly renounce heliocentrism, kneeling before the Inquisition to read his recantation. But it is said that after reading it he murmured under his breath: “And yet it moves.”
consequences: Galileo was placed under house arrest until his death but preserved his life. During house arrest he continued his research in secret and completed Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences. It took the Church 300 years to admit its error. Galileo’s choice has been seen by some as pragmatic and by others as a betrayal of the truth.
choice_support_a: Understanding Galileo: only by preserving freedom and life could he continue his research; martyrdom would mean nothing for science, and truth will ultimately prevail over lies (Freedom > Truth)
choice_support_b: Criticizing Galileo: as a scientist, he should have given his life for the truth; publicly renouncing the truth was a betrayal of science (Truth > Freedom)
reflection: If you were Galileo, would you choose martyrdom for the truth, or temporary submission to preserve the chance to continue your research?

title: Angel Heart: Tacitly Allowing an Unauthorized Kidney Removal to Save Your Daughter?
real_person: Liu Chenxi (character in the TV drama Angel Heart)
context: In the TV drama Angel Heart, the doctor Liu Chenxi’s daughter Nannan suffers from severe kidney disease, her condition steadily worsening as she waits for a suitable kidney. A boy in the hospital dies despite resuscitation efforts; his kidney matches Nannan’s, but the boy’s parents explicitly refuse to donate. Colleagues, eager to save Nannan, try to obtain the kidney by bypassing the family’s consent, and even prepare to give Liu Chenxi a sedative and do it on his behalf. When Liu Chenxi finds out, the question before him is not whether he could plan a kidney removal himself, but whether he should stop the people around him.
dilemma: Suppose you are this father: your daughter may not live to see another transplant opportunity, and your colleagues are already prepared to take a kidney in secret. You need only turn a blind eye to win your daughter a chance at life; but that means accepting an organ obtained without consent, knowing another family has already refused. Would you stop them, or tacitly allow them to continue?
actual_choice: In the drama, Liu Chenxi stops his colleagues, and Nannan does not receive this transplant. He did not turn the other family’s right to refuse donation into an obstacle that could be bypassed simply because his daughter needed it.
consequences: This time, Liu Chenxi respected the deceased’s family’s refusal, but his daughter lost the transplant opportunity before her and still had to wait as her condition worsened. The cost here is the loss of one chance at life, not that his daughter had already died as a result; at the moment of choosing, he could not be sure whether another kidney would ever come.
choice_support_a: Stop the unauthorized kidney removal: you cannot violate another family’s explicit refusal to donate just because your own child needs it, even if your daughter may lose a chance at life (Justice > Family)
choice_support_b: Tacitly allow colleagues to take the kidney: accept a kidney obtained without consent to win your daughter a chance to live, even if this violates another family’s rights (Family > Justice)
reflection: The other family’s child is already dead, while your child can still be saved. At this moment, can you still hold to “saving a life does not justify seizing an organ”?

title: Should Hank Investigate His Brother-in-Law Walter, the Drug Kingpin?
real_person: Hank and Walter (characters in the TV series Breaking Bad)
context: DEA agent Hank and his brother-in-law Walter (their wives are sisters) had been close for years: the two families gathered often and cared for each other’s children together; after Walter was diagnosed with cancer, Hank always regarded him as family in need of protection. Later Hank discovered that the drug-manufacturing kingpin he had pursued for years, “Heisenberg,” was Walter himself. By then Walter had left the drug business, but his cancer had recurred. He told Hank that even if the investigation continued, he would probably be dead by the time the case was solved. Exposing him would not stop someone currently committing crimes, but it would cost Walter’s wife and two children their family; the children would have to know their father was a drug kingpin and a killer, and the entire family’s reputation and life would be destroyed. The cost of Hank’s rehabilitation after being shot actually came from Walter’s drug money, and Hank himself might come under investigation. But during the years Walter built his drug empire, he had caused and taken part in multiple deaths, protecting himself through threats, deception, and killing. If Hank stayed silent, Walter might escape all accountability thanks to his cancer and family ties, and the victims would never get justice.
dilemma: Should you keep silent about Walter — terminally ill and already out of the business — in order to protect innocent family members (Family), or insist that he face investigation and trial for the deaths and harm he caused (Justice)?
actual_choice: Hank chose to continue the investigation and ultimately arrested Walter with his own hands in the desert.
consequences: Just as Hank finished handcuffing Walter, a group of armed drug traffickers arrived; Hank was killed in the exchange of fire.
choice_support_a: Uphold justice: a family relationship cannot be an indulgence for a drug kingpin. No matter how much time Walter has left, he must face investigation and trial for the deaths and harm he caused (Justice > Family)
choice_support_b: Protect the family: Walter has already left crime and is about to die. Continuing the investigation can only destroy his wife’s and children’s lives, making the whole family pay for his crimes (Family > Justice)
reflection: If a relative who has committed serious crimes has stopped offending and is terminally ill, and the most direct consequence of exposing him is destroying the lives of other innocent family members, would you still insist on holding him accountable?

title: Qu Yang and Liu Zhengfeng: Friends Who Truly Understood Each Other
real_person: Qu Yang and Liu Zhengfeng (characters in Jin Yong’s novel The Smiling, Proud Wanderer)
context: In Jin Yong’s novel The Smiling, Proud Wanderer, Elder Liu Zhengfeng of the Mount Heng Sect and Elder Qu Yang of the Sun Moon Holy Cult belong to the orthodox and heterodox camps respectively, yet they became kindred spirits through their shared love of music. They played together and compiled the score of The Smiling, Proud Wanderer, but each camp regarded the other as an enemy, and sect relations did not permit them to associate openly. Liu Zhengfeng therefore decided to wash his hands of the world and withdraw from the sect conflicts of the martial world.
dilemma: If your sect demanded that you cut off contact with a friend from an enemy sect, would you obey your sect and uphold the organization’s boundaries, or insist on your right to choose your own friends and pursue art? The former means preserving your sect identity; the latter may be seen as betraying your sect.
actual_choice: Liu Zhengfeng did not completely sever his friendship with Qu Yang according to sect order, and Qu Yang did not give up the relationship because of the divide between orthodox and heterodox. Faced with pressure to break off contact and give an account of their relationship, the two still chose to complete the score of The Smiling, Proud Wanderer together and leave the conflicts of the sects.
consequences: The two lost their original sect identities and standing in the martial world, and paid with their lives; but they preserved the right to choose their friends, pursue music, and decide how to live. The story thus raises the question: can sect loyalty demand that a person give up true friendship and spiritual life?
choice_support_a: Supporting Qu Yang and Liu Zhengfeng: sect identity should not dictate whom a person may associate with or what art they may appreciate. Freely choosing friends and a way of life is more important than obeying an exclusionary organization’s commands (Freedom > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Supporting sect order: joining an organization means accepting its corresponding boundaries and obligations; one cannot enjoy sect identity while refusing to comply with the organization’s requirements regarding friend and enemy relations (Loyalty > Freedom)
reflection: If your organization demanded that you cut off relations with your most important friend, would you obey the organization or keep your own choice?

title: DDT and Malaria Control
context: In 1948, the Swiss chemist Paul Müller won the Nobel Prize for inventing the insecticide DDT. After World War II, DDT was used on a massive scale to control malaria, saving millions of lives. But by the 1960s, scientists had found that DDT accumulates in organisms, causing thinning bird eggshells, endangered species, and ecosystem damage. Environmentalists demanded a total ban on DDT, but tropical countries faced a dilemma: banning DDT would cause malaria to resurge.
dilemma: Should DDT be completely banned to protect the ecological environment, even if this would cause millions to die of malaria; or should DDT continue to be used to save lives, even if this would cause long-term environmental damage?
actual_choice: Developed countries largely banned DDT in the 1970s. But malaria-endemic regions such as Africa continued restricted use of DDT for indoor spraying as a last-resort anti-epidemic measure.
consequences: Bird populations in developed countries gradually recovered. But in Africa, hundreds of thousands still die of malaria every year, most of them children. In 2006 the WHO re-endorsed DDT for malaria control. The debate over “whether to save lives now or protect the ecology in the long run” continues to this day.
choice_support_a: Supporting continued use of DDT: saving human lives is more important than protecting birds; children in poor countries must not pay for the environmental ideals of rich countries (Life > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Supporting a ban on DDT: once an ecosystem collapses, it will cause even larger-scale loss of life; alternatives should be found rather than drinking poison to quench thirst (Environmental Protection > Life)
reflection: If your child lived in a malaria-endemic area, would you support banning DDT?

title: Xu Bingchuan Is Publicly Tried and Executed
real_person: Xu Bingchuan and the Baoshan County land-reform work team
location: Fengtang Township, Baoshan County, Shanghai, China
context: During the land reform of 1950–1952, landlords were classified as a class to be remolded and eliminated. Xu Bingchuan, known locally as “Xiao Bingchuan,” of Fengtang Township in Baoshan County, Shanghai, was identified in land-reform records as a landlord who oppressed hired laborers and had the character of a “local tyrant.” At the public trial, his wife also took the stage to accuse him. The extant materials record these accusations and the execution process, but the class designation made during the campaign cannot be equated directly with criminal facts confirmed by an independent trial.
dilemma: You are a member of the land-reform work team. The masses demand the execution of a man identified as a “tyrant landlord,” believing that unless he is killed the land reform cannot be completed and other landlords will continue to resist. But the available evidence comes mainly from mass accusations, class status, and political review, and is not sufficient to prove every charge. Do you obey the revolutionary faith that class enemies must be eliminated, or suspend the execution and give priority to protecting the life of one specific person?
actual_choice: The local land-reform work team accepted the class and political designation of Xu Bingchuan. He was sentenced to death at the public trial and then shot.
consequences: The execution reinforced revolutionary authority in the land reform and showed local people the punitive boundary of class struggle; but one person’s life was irrevocably handed over to a class label, mass mobilization, and political review. This case leaves an unavoidable question: in order to build an ideal society, can those defined as enemies first be treated as objects that must be sacrificed?
choice_support_a: Supporting the execution: the landlord class had relied on exploitation and violence to oppress peasants; without thoroughly eliminating the most dangerous local tyrants, land reform could not be completed, the old order could not be broken, and a new society could not be built (Revolutionary Faith > Life)
choice_support_b: Opposing the execution: regardless of a person’s class origin or how the masses judge him, his life cannot be taken without independent evidence and a normal trial; social reform cannot use treating people as class enemies as an excuse to kill (Life > Revolutionary Faith)
reflection: If you believed that eliminating class oppression was the necessary path to an ideal society, but this particular person’s specific crimes had not been established through an independent trial, would you approve the execution?

title: Surveillance for Everyone, in the Name of Safety?
real_person: Public security bureaus in multiple parts of China (Police Cloud)
location: Shandong, Jiangsu, Tianjin, and other parts of China
context: You are responsible for public safety in a city. To detect violent crime and other dangers in advance, the police want to pool information that was previously scattered: people's WeChat, Weibo, and QQ accounts and online activity, shopping and delivery records, accommodation, travel, and location data, and whom they travel with and which internet cafes they frequent. The vast majority of people are not suspected of any crime, but the system can use this information to identify those flagged as “key persons” and their associates. The broader the collection, the more likely leads can be found in advance—and the harder it is for ordinary people to know when they are being monitored or why they have been listed as a risk.
dilemma: Should the police be allowed to continuously pool ordinary people's digital lives so that potential threats can be identified before danger occurs; or should you insist that without specific suspicion, no one and their social connections should be placed under surveillance, even if that might miss warning signs?
actual_choice: Public security bureaus in multiple parts of China have built a “Police Cloud.” Based on procurement documents from Shandong, Jiangsu, Tianjin, and other places, Human Rights Watch found that the system integrates government records, online accounts and activity, shopping and logistics, and travel information to track “key persons” and their associates; those targeted include petitioners and people deemed potentially capable of affecting “stability.” Independent technical research has also confirmed that WeChat censors the text and images of one-on-one and group chats for accounts registered in China, and that sensitive messages may fail to be delivered without the sender being notified. Weibo, Douyin, Xiaohongshu, and other platforms have also been documented deleting posts, limiting the visibility of content, or banning accounts; some people have been summoned by police or detained over online speech. These are censorship and law-enforcement practices of different platforms and departments, and cannot all be attributed to a single “Police Cloud” system.
consequences: Data collection on this scale gives the police the ability to look for leads in everyday behavior, but ordinary people may also come into the surveillance net because they traveled with someone under scrutiny or had some other connection. When private messages are sent but the recipient cannot see them, posts are deleted or their spread is restricted, accounts are banned, and people are summoned over their speech, everyday communication carries real risks. Those flagged find it difficult to learn why or to appeal; personal privacy, the presumption of innocence, and freedom of association may all be damaged. Public investigations have documented cross-platform content censorship and cross-source data collection in multiple locations, but it has not been confirmed that every private message on every app nationwide is reviewed one by one by state security departments.
choice_support_a: Insist on Justice: without specific suspicion and effective oversight, the accounts, shopping, travel, and social connections of ordinary people should not be pooled on a massive scale and innocent people treated as potential risks, even if warning signs may be missed (Justice > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Insist on Public Safety: the earlier danger is identified, the more likely innocent people can be protected; to that end, ordinary people's digital footprints may be integrated and suspicious connections investigated in advance, even if most of those under surveillance have never broken the law (Public Safety > Justice)
reflection: If you have always believed that public safety should come first, when your own chat accounts, shopping records, and travel connections are also drawn into risk analysis, are you still willing to have everyone accept this kind of surveillance?

title: After His Wife and Daughters Were Held in North Korea
real_person: Oh Kil-nam, Shin Suk-ja, and their two daughters
location: West Germany, Denmark, and North Korea
context: In 1985, the South Korean economist Oh Kil-nam moved to North Korea with his wife, Shin Suk-ja, and their two young daughters. The following year, the North Korean authorities sent him to West Germany to recruit South Korean students. He sought political asylum in Denmark and did not return as ordered. After that, his wife and daughters were detained by the North Korean authorities; the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found their detention to be arbitrary. The North Korean regime used his family's situation to pressure Oh Kil-nam, demanding that he return and continue working for the regime.
dilemma: You have already escaped to a free country, but your wife and two daughters are being held by the regime. You could go back and work for the regime again, hoping your family will be released as a result; but once back, you might lose your freedom again, and the regime has not guaranteed that it will let them go. Will you return to serve in order to be reunited with your wife and daughters, or stay in a free land and bear the pain of your family remaining imprisoned while you cannot be with them?
actual_choice: Oh Kil-nam did not return to North Korea. He applied for political asylum in Denmark and later returned to South Korea. The North Korean authorities did not release his wife and daughters; for many years afterward, he continued to call for reunion with his family.
consequences: Oh Kil-nam kept his freedom and was no longer forced to work for the North Korean regime, but his wife and daughters were imprisoned for a long time, separated from him. In 2012, North Korea stated that Shin Suk-ja had died and that the daughters did not wish to contact their father, but provided no independently verifiable time or place of death; the UN Working Group demanded that North Korea immediately release the detained wife and daughters. Reunion never happened, and whether returning could have saved his family remains an unanswered question.
choice_support_a: Insist on Freedom: do not return to serve a regime that persecutes your family. Even if your wife and daughters remain detained, the regime must not be allowed to use family ties to force you to give up your freedom; going back does not guarantee their release (Freedom > Family)
choice_support_b: Choose Family: your wife and two daughters are being held, and you cannot simply look after yourself by staying in a safe place; even if returning may cost you your freedom again, you must fight for the chance to be reunited with your family (Family > Freedom)
reflection: If a regime held your spouse and young children and demanded that you return to work for it, without guaranteeing your family's release, would you go back?

title: Martin Luther King Jr. Rejects the Communists
context: In 1965, the civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. faced a difficult choice. The FBI threatened him: if he did not cut ties with Communist sympathizers in the movement and publicly denounce the radical left, it would expose scandals from his private life. Communist supporters had long been important allies of the civil rights movement, providing substantial funding and organizational support for the struggle for Black rights. But King feared that being labeled a “Red” would destroy the entire civil rights movement.
dilemma: Should he remain loyal to allies and comrades, even if this could be used to attack the movement; or should he cut ties with certain allies for the sake of a larger ideal (racial equality)?
actual_choice: King chose to distance himself from the radical left, publicly emphasizing the nonviolent and Christian character of the civil rights movement and drawing a line against communism. Some radicals who had once fought alongside him left the movement as a result.
consequences: King's strategy won broader middle-class support for the civil rights movement and ultimately helped bring about the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. But he was criticized by radicals for “betraying” his allies, and some left-wing activists believed that he had compromised with power.
choice_support_a: Understand King's choice: to achieve a larger goal (racial equality), tactical compromises are necessary, and loyalty should not stand in the way of realizing an ideal (Faith/Ideal > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Criticize King's choice: abandoning comrades who fought alongside you under pressure is betrayal; loyalty and solidarity are the foundation of a movement (Loyalty > Faith)
reflection: If you were the leader of the movement, would you cut ties with radical allies for the sake of strategic success?

title: The Terri Schiavo Right-to-Die Case
context: In 2005, Terri Schiavo, an American woman who had suffered severe brain damage after cardiac arrest, had been in a vegetative state for 15 years. Her husband, Michael, believed that his wife would not want to live in a vegetative state and asked the hospital to remove her feeding tube so that she could pass away peacefully. But Terri's parents adamantly opposed this, believing that as long as she was alive there was hope, and they demanded that their daughter's life be maintained.
dilemma: When a family is divided, should the patient's likely wishes be respected and she be allowed to pass away peacefully, or should life be sustained at all costs until natural death?
actual_choice: After years of legal battle, the courts ultimately upheld the husband's decision and allowed the feeding tube to be removed. On March 31, 2005, Terri died with her parents at her side.
consequences: The case triggered a great debate in American society and even drew in Congress and the President. Her parents to this day believe that the husband “murdered” their daughter. The case prompted more Americans to start signing living wills, making clear their wishes regarding life-sustaining treatment.
choice_support_a: Support the husband: a vegetative state is meaningless, and letting the patient leave with dignity matters more than sustaining a life devoid of any quality (Dignity of Life > Attachment to Family)
choice_support_b: Support the parents: as long as there is even a spark of life, it should not be given up, and parents have the right to fight for every day of their child's survival (Family > Quality of Life)
reflection: If your own relative became a vegetative patient, would you choose to remove the tube or to keep them alive?

title: Revealing the Truth of Chernobyl
context: After the 1986 explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, the chief scientist Valery Legasov discovered that the cause of the accident was a design flaw in the reactor, and that more than a dozen other Soviet reactors of the same type had the same hidden danger. The Soviet authorities demanded that he conceal the design flaw from the International Atomic Energy Agency and admit only that it had been an operational error, in order to protect the reputation of the Soviet nuclear industry and “social stability.” But Legasov knew that concealing the truth meant other reactors could repeat the disaster at any time.
dilemma: Should he obey the national interest and conceal the defects in the nuclear facilities in order to preserve social stability, or should he disregard the consequences and reveal the truth to prevent a future disaster?
actual_choice: Legasov partly complied with the official line at the international conference, but privately recorded tapes revealing the truth. In 1988, on the second anniversary of the accident, he took his own life at home, leaving behind testimony exposing the systemic problems of the Soviet nuclear industry.
consequences: After his death, Legasov's tapes circulated and prompted the Soviet Union to improve the safety design of its nuclear power plants. But he himself was suppressed by the authorities and stripped of the honors he deserved. The HBO series Chernobyl introduced the world to this scientist who sacrificed himself for the truth.
choice_support_a: Admire Legasov: a scientist's duty is to reveal the truth; concealing safety hazards may lead to an even greater disaster, and truth comes before stability (Truth > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Understand the official position: against the backdrop of the Cold War, exposing defects in nuclear facilities could trigger panic and endanger national security, so stability comes first (Public Safety > Truth)
reflection: If you discovered a dangerous truth, would you risk revealing it or obey an order to cover it up?

title: Julia Butterfly Hill's Tree Protest
context: In 1997, the 23-year-old environmental activist Julia climbed a 55-meter-tall ancient tree to protest the logging of thousand-year-old redwoods, vowing not to come down until her goal was achieved. Her family begged her to come down: “Your parents need you; you can't abandon your family for a tree.” But Julia believed that these ancient trees were an irreplaceable ecological heritage. She built a simple platform in the tree and survived on food hauled up by rope.
dilemma: Should she return to the ground to care for the family that needs her, or continue a dangerous tree protest for the environmental cause, even though her family is frightened and worried for her?
actual_choice: Julia stayed in the tree for 738 days (more than two years), enduring storms, freezing winters, and harassment from the logging company. She refused every request to come down, including her family's pleas.
consequences: In 1999, the timber company finally compromised, promising to permanently protect the tree and the surrounding grove. Julia became an environmental hero, but her relationship with her family was severely strained. Her mother publicly said that she could not understand her daughter's behavior of “abandoning her family for a tree.”
choice_support_a: Support Julia: thousand-year-old trees are an irreplaceable ecological heritage, and sacrificing for the environment is a meaningful sacrifice (Environmental Protection > Family)
choice_support_b: Sympathize with the family: environmental protection matters, but it should not come at the cost of abandoning one's family; parents do not raise children so that they can risk their lives in a tree for two years (Family > Environmental Protection)
reflection: If your child took extreme action for the environmental cause, would you support it or oppose it?

title: Jiang Yanyong Exposes the Cover-Up of the SARS Outbreak
context: During the 2003 SARS outbreak, the officially announced number of cases in Beijing was far lower than the actual situation, and cases at military hospitals were also not fully included in public statistics. Jiang Yanyong, then a military doctor, disclosed to the media that military hospitals had admitted a large number of SARS patients, which brought international attention to the epidemic information. Reports from the same period showed that military personnel needed approval from the political department to be interviewed by foreign media; however, the available material cannot confirm that he had received an explicit, individual prohibition before his disclosure.
dilemma: As a military doctor, will you obey the Party's and the military's information management and organizational discipline and not disclose to the outside world the epidemic information held by military hospitals; or will you go beyond organizational restrictions and make the case situation public so that the public and health agencies can promptly recognize the risk of transmission?
actual_choice: Jiang Yanyong disclosed the SARS cases at military hospitals to the media. On April 20, 2003, the Chinese authorities sharply raised the official Beijing case numbers and shifted to daily reporting and strengthened prevention and control; his disclosure helped draw attention, but was not the sole reason for the subsequent changes in the response.
consequences: Making the information public brought the previously underreported scale of the epidemic into public and international view and helped reveal the seriousness of the delayed reporting. In 2004, Jiang Yanyong was detained for nearly seven weeks for demanding a reassessment of the 1989 Tiananmen events, and after his release he faced restrictions on interviews and surveillance; this later repression had a clear political context and should not be simply attributed to his SARS whistleblowing.
choice_support_a: Support Loyalty: comply with the Party's and the military's information management requirements and uphold organizational discipline and the chain of command; soldiers should not disclose internal information to the outside without authorization, even if this means that the public cannot, for the time being, learn the full extent of the epidemic (Loyalty > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Support Public Safety: epidemic information is crucial to infectious disease prevention and control, and delayed disclosure hinders the public and health agencies from assessing risk; even if it violates the Party's and the military's information management requirements, the scale of the epidemic should be revealed promptly (Public Safety > Loyalty)
reflection: When the Party and the military require compliance with epidemic information management, and delayed disclosure may hinder infectious disease prevention and control, will you put organizational discipline or public safety first?

title: Defending Suiyang: Loyalty at the Cost of the People's Lives?
real_person: Zhang Xun, Xu Yuan, and the soldiers and people of Suiyang
context: During the An Lushan Rebellion, Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan led troops in defending Suiyang against the rebel army, tying down its advance toward the Jianghuai region. The city was besieged for a long time, reinforcements never arrived, and the food ran out. The defenders did not stop resisting; instead, they kept fighting by killing and eating the city's residents. Later generations praised their loyal sacrifice for holding Suiyang for the Tang, but the cost of this loyalty was not only the soldiers' own lives, but also those of the city's people.
dilemma: You are the defending general, charged with resisting the rebels and defending the country. The food is gone, and continuing to hold the city requires killing civilians to feed the soldiers. Will you refuse to feed on the people, even if that means you cannot continue to hold the city and may be seen as disloyal; or will you, rather than submit to the rebels, allow the people to be sacrificed in order to sustain the resistance? Stopping the resistance does not guarantee that the enemy will spare soldiers and civilians, but continuing to kill and eat civilians means that you are actively taking their lives.
actual_choice: According to the Old Book of Tang and other records, Zhang Xun killed his own concubine and forced the soldiers to eat her; the defenders then killed and ate the city's women and other residents and continued to resist the rebels. Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan did not give up defending the city. In 757, Suiyang finally fell; Zhang Xun was captured and killed, and Xu Yuan was taken away and later also killed.
consequences: The city's civilians were killed and eaten, and the defense ultimately did not prevent the city from falling. Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan were later honored as loyal martyrs for tying down the rebels and shielding the Jianghuai region, but sustaining the resistance with the lives of innocents also makes this defense a question about the limits of loyalty: a general may choose to die for his country, but does he also have the right to decide sacrifices on behalf of the people?
choice_support_a: Hold the line on Life: refuse to kill and eat civilians; even if you cannot continue to hold the city, you must not, in order to fulfill loyalty, actively kill the people you are supposed to protect. That you are willing to die for your country does not mean that you have the right to demand that others sacrifice themselves (Life > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Insist on defending the city for the country: Suiyang is vital to the safety of the Jianghuai region, and you cannot submit to the rebels just because the food has run out; even if it requires the lives of the city's people, you must sustain the resistance and fulfill your duty to defend the country (Loyalty > Life)
reflection: If the price of loyalty to your country were killing the people you are supposed to protect, would you still call this kind of perseverance loyalty?

title: Charles Darwin Publishes the Theory of Evolution
context: In 1859, Darwin completed On the Origin of Species, setting out the theory of evolution. But he well knew that this theory would shake the foundations of the Christian creation account and depart from the religious faith he had held since childhood. His wife, Emma, a devout Christian, begged him not to publish a theory that “blasphemed God.” Darwin was torn by 20 years of painful hesitation: should he hold fast to his religious faith and protect family harmony, or publish a scientific truth that overturned faith?
dilemma: When scientific discovery conflicts with religious faith, should the truth be suppressed in order to preserve faith, or should faith be challenged for the sake of truth, even if that damages family relationships and betrays a lifelong belief?
actual_choice: Darwin ultimately chose to publish the theory of evolution. On November 24, 1859, On the Origin of Species was published, and the first printing of 1,250 copies sold out that day.
consequences: The theory of evolution provoked enormous controversy, and the Church condemned Darwin as a “heretic.” His relationship with his wife was strained, and he felt guilty for the rest of his life over departing from his faith. But evolution became the foundation of modern biology and fundamentally changed humanity's understanding of itself. On his deathbed, Darwin was still reproaching himself for “harming his wife's faith.”
choice_support_a: Sympathize with his wife: faith is a person's spiritual pillar, and destroying a family member's belief system for the sake of a scientific theory is cruel (Faith > Truth)
choice_support_b: Support Darwin: scientific truth should not be suppressed by religious faith; the pursuit of truth is the foundation of human progress (Truth > Faith)
reflection: If your scientific discovery would overturn the religious faith of you and your family, would you publish it?

title: Batman Takes the Blame for Harvey Dent
real_person: Batman and James Gordon (characters in the film The Dark Knight)
location: Gotham City (a fictional city in the film; 2008 is the year of release)
context: In the 2008 film The Dark Knight, the district attorney Harvey Dent fights crime through the justice system and becomes a symbol for Gotham's citizens that justice can be achieved and that the city can change. But after being struck down by the Joker, he turns to vengeance and commits murder. After Dent's death, Batman and Gordon know of his crimes, and they also fear that if the truth were made public, citizens would see the collapse of this hero as the failure of the entire ideal of judicial reform. The belief that needs to be upheld here is not loyalty to Dent as an individual, but the hope that ordinary people can change society through public justice.
dilemma: If you were Batman, would you have Gordon make Dent's crimes public, so that citizens and the victims' families know who the real killer was; or would you take the blame yourself and ask Gordon to conceal the truth, preserving Dent's image as a hero of judicial reform? The former respects the public's right to know the facts, but may shake the beliefs they have only just established; the latter tries to preserve a shared hope, but makes the public believe something false and turns you into a hunted man. Whether making the truth public would necessarily destroy hope is the character's judgment, not an established fact.
actual_choice: Batman chose to take the blame for Dent and let Gordon hunt him as the killer. Gordon did not reveal Dent's killings to the public, but continued to call him a hero in his eulogy. Batman was willing to lose his own reputation and become a hunted man in order to preserve the symbol of justice and change in the citizens' hearts.
consequences: Dent's heroic image was preserved, while Batman was hunted; the public and the victims' families never learned who the real killer was. The two hoped that this lie would sustain citizens' belief in judicial reform, but it cannot therefore be asserted that publicizing the facts would necessarily destroy the ideal. While preserving hope, they also decided on the public's behalf which facts should not be known, making this shared belief depend on a false heroic image.
choice_support_a: Preserve belief: let Batman take the blame and conceal Dent's crimes. The collapse of one man must not be allowed to destroy an entire city's belief that justice can be achieved and that society can change; when people have only just begun to believe in these ideals, preserving a shared hope matters more than immediately revealing the facts (Faith > Truth)
choice_support_b: Make the truth public: let the public and the victims' families know Dent's crimes, and do not pin the blame on Batman. People have the right to judge heroes and institutions on the basis of facts; an ideal truly worth upholding should withstand the test of facts rather than be sustained by concealment (Truth > Faith)
reflection: When a hero who sustains many people's beliefs commits a crime, will you make the facts public and let the ideal be tested, or conceal his failure and preserve people's hope of continuing to believe in justice?

title: The Jury Verdict in the Simpson Case
context: In 1995, the American football star O.J. Simpson was charged with murdering his ex-wife. The evidence, including blood DNA and a glove, scientifically almost proved his guilt. But the defense exposed the Los Angeles Police Department's history of racial discrimination and violations in evidence collection. The jury (mostly Black) faced a choice: convict on the basis of scientific evidence, or use an acquittal to punish a police department with a history of racism and to “avenge” the countless Black people wrongfully convicted throughout history?
dilemma: Should the jury be loyal to the evidence and the truth and reach a verdict that may be correct, or should it use this opportunity to send a signal to an unjust system, even if that may let the real perpetrator go free?
actual_choice: After less than four hours of deliberation, the jury acquitted Simpson. Several jurors later admitted that they knew Simpson might be guilty, but that acquitting him was “revenge” against the police department's racism.
consequences: The verdict divided American society: most white people considered it a miscarriage of justice, while most Black people cheered it. Simpson gained his freedom but was ruined in reputation. The case became a classic controversy over “whether a jury should decide a case on political motives rather than evidence.” In 1997, a civil lawsuit found that Simpson had to pay $33.5 million in damages.
choice_support_a: Support the jury: in the face of systemic racial injustice, this verdict was a correction of historical injustice, and social justice is higher than the truth of an individual case (Justice > Truth)
choice_support_b: Criticize the verdict: the judicial system should look only at evidence and truth; using a wrongful verdict to take revenge on the system undermines the rule of law (Truth > Justice)
reflection: If you were a juror, would you decide the case on the basis of evidence or on considerations of social justice?

title: Life Is Beautiful: Describing a Concentration Camp as a Game
real_person: Guido and his son Giosuè (characters in the film Life Is Beautiful)
location: A Nazi concentration camp (film setting; released in 1997)
context: In the 1997 film Life Is Beautiful, a Jewish father, Guido, and his young son, Giosuè, are sent to a Nazi concentration camp. So that the child will not be crushed by fear—and to fit with his own protective arrangements—Guido pretends that they are taking part in a game: if they do not cry, do not complain of hunger, and hide according to the rules, they will earn points; with a thousand points, they can win a real tank. The lie here is not told to the enemy, but to make the child he deeply loves believe in a story completely different from reality.
dilemma: You are this father. You could tell the child that they are imprisoned in a place where people are killed, and that hiding and staying silent are for survival, so that he understands the real danger; but this might also make him panic and lose hope. You could also invent a game with a prize, so that he cooperates with the hiding out of expectation, but that prevents him from truly understanding his situation. Will you let the child face the truth, or use a well-intentioned lie to fight for a chance to protect his life?
actual_choice: Guido chose to maintain the lie of the game. He did not understand German, but pretended to translate the guards' orders, turning threats into game rules. When the camp was being evacuated, he hid his son and told him that this was the final test before winning the tank, and that he must not come out until everyone had left. As Guido was being taken away by guards, he still performed funny antics for his hidden son, continuing to make him believe that it was only a game; Guido was then killed.
consequences: The son followed the hiding arrangements and lived until the next day. When an American tank entered the camp, he thought that he had truly won the prize, and later he was reunited with his surviving mother. The lie in the film not only eased fear but also encouraged the child to stay quiet and keep hiding, playing a real role in protecting his life; but his survival also depended on his father's protection and the arrival of the Allies, and cannot be attributed to the lie alone. As an adult, the son understood his father's sacrifice in the narration.
choice_support_a: Protect Life: use the lie of a game and a prize to sustain the child's hope and make him cooperate with hiding and keep waiting; in an extreme crisis, he may temporarily be made to believe in a fictional reality in order to fight for a chance to survive (Life > Truth)
choice_support_b: Face the Truth: explain the real danger in a way the child can understand, so that he knows why he must hide well; do not package a deadly threat as a game—even if facing reality may frighten him, it helps him act on the basis of his real situation (Truth > Life)
reflection: If a fictional story could keep a child hopeful and cooperating to survive, but would prevent him from understanding the real danger he faces, would you keep up the lie?

title: Manila's Black Nazarene Procession Under a Terror Alert
real_person: Organizers of the Quiapo Church and the pilgrims
context: In January 2012, Philippine President Aquino publicly warned that the intelligence services had received reports that terrorists might attack the Black Nazarene procession; the Quiapo Church also said that it had received information containing the names of suspected attackers. Both the government and the Church discussed canceling the event, but the credibility of the intelligence was questioned, and police searches found no bombs or explosives. Facing the risk of millions of devotees gathering and the possibility of mass casualties if an attack occurred, the organizers still decided to hold the procession.
dilemma: When a terror alert aimed at millions of people is unconfirmed but could cause heavy casualties if it came true, would you cancel or postpone an important religious procession, or continue it after strengthening security?
actual_choice: The church organizers did not cancel the procession. On January 9, 2012, millions of devotees took part under a large police deployment; the procession lasted about 22 hours, and in the end no terrorist attack occurred.
consequences: The procession ended peacefully, with no bomb attack; but this does not prove that the risk beforehand was zero. The Red Cross treated several hundred devotees for minor injuries, fatigue, dehydration, and fainting. The core trade-off that the event left behind is: maintain an important collective religious practice, or avoid gathering an extremely large crowd when the risk of a terror attack has not been ruled out.
choice_support_a: Insist on holding it: for the devotees, the Feast of the Black Nazarene is an important collective practice of faith; when the threat is unconfirmed and the security forces have already been greatly strengthened, continuing to hold it does not necessarily amount to disregarding life (Faith > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Cancel or postpone: when millions gather, even if the attack intelligence is uncertain, the potential casualties could be extremely severe; postponing the event can avoid putting the public at preventable risk (Public Safety > Faith)
reflection: If a terror alert has limited credibility but could affect millions of participants, would you insist on holding an important religious event, or first cancel it to protect the public?

title: Ganges Pollution and the Livelihoods of the Poor in India
context: In 1985, the Indian government faced a crisis of Ganges pollution. The main sources of pollution were small leather factories and dyeing workshops, which employed millions of poor workers. The environmental protection department recommended forcibly closing all substandard small factories in order to restore the water quality of the Ganges. But this meant that millions of workers at the bottom of society would lose their jobs; with no other skills for making a living, they would fall into extreme poverty. Prime Minister Gandhi faced a choice: environmental protection first, or social justice first?
dilemma: Should the polluting factories be closed in order to restore the ecology of the sacred river, even if this throws millions of poor people out of work; or should the livelihoods of the poor be protected, even if that means continued pollution?
actual_choice: The Gandhi government adopted a gradual policy: mandatory environmental requirements for large factories, but longer grace periods and financial support for small workshops, avoiding a one-size-fits-all approach that would cause mass unemployment.
consequences: Ganges pollution improved slowly and remains a serious problem today. But social unrest and mass extreme poverty were avoided. The case became a classic example of the “conflict between environmental protection and social justice”: developed countries can sacrifice the economy in pursuit of environmental protection, but poor people in developing countries cannot pay for environmental protection with their survival.
choice_support_a: Support social justice first: the poor must not be made to pay for environmental protection; employment and the right to survive come before the environment (Justice/Livelihood > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Insist on environmental protection first: Ganges pollution affects the health of hundreds of millions of people, and protecting the environment is justice for more people (Environmental Protection > Employment for a Few)
reflection: If closing polluting factories would put poor people out of work, would you force them to close?

title: China Bans Motorcycles to Tackle Smog
context: In 2002, Beijing decided to ban motorcycles from the roads to tackle air pollution, and later also restricted vehicles from other regions and implemented an odd-even license plate rule. Millions of migrant workers, delivery riders, and couriers who depended on motorcycles to get to work protested that this violated their freedom of movement. The government insisted that tackling smog was in the public interest and that individuals must make sacrifices.
dilemma: Should citizens' right to freely choose their means of transport be protected, or should individual freedom of movement be restricted for the collective environmental interest?
actual_choice: The government enforced the motorcycle ban and traffic restrictions, confiscating tens of thousands of motorcycles. Protesters were dispersed, and the policy was strictly enforced.
consequences: Beijing's air quality improved significantly over the following decade (though other factors were also at work, of course). But hundreds of thousands of low-income workers were forced to change how they commuted, at greatly increased cost and time. Critics called it an “environmental dictatorship” at the expense of the rights and interests of the poor.
choice_support_a: Criticize the policy: depriving the poor of their means of livelihood without compensation is unjust, and environmental protection should not be paid for by those at the bottom (Freedom/Justice > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Support the government: environmental pollution endangers everyone's health, and restricting a minority's freedom of movement is necessary (Environmental Protection > Freedom)
reflection: For the sake of environmental protection, may individual freedom of movement be forcibly restricted?

title: The 2002 Moscow Theater Hostage Crisis
context: In 2002, Chechen terrorists seized a Moscow theater and took 850 hostages, threatening to detonate explosives. Negotiations reached a deadlock. The Russian special forces had two options: continue negotiating, which might preserve more hostages' lives, but the terrorists might actually detonate the explosives; or storm the building, which would certainly cause hostage casualties, but would ensure that the terrorists did not succeed and would deter future terrorism.
