dilemma: Should priority be given to protecting the lives of the current hostages by negotiating as long as possible, or should there be a hardline anti-terror response that does not yield to terrorism, even if that leads to the deaths of some hostages?
actual_choice: Putin ordered the storming. The special forces released an anesthetic gas into the theater and rushed in, killing all the terrorists, but 129 hostages died from overdoses of the anesthetic.
consequences: More than 120 hostages died from the military's anesthetic gas. Putin refused to apologize, saying, “We saved more people and showed the terrorists that Russia will not compromise.” Critics believe that the government sacrificed innocent hostages; supporters believe that it deterred terrorism and protected long-term security.
choice_support_a: Criticize the government: the government's duty is to protect citizens' lives, and a decision that led to the deaths of 120 hostages was a failure (Life > Security Lessons)
choice_support_b: Support the storming: yielding to terrorism encourages more attacks, and a hardline anti-terror response has protected more lives in the future (Public Safety > Some Lives in the Present)
reflection: If you were the leader, would you give priority to saving the hostages in front of you or to deterring future terrorism?

title: Can a Victim Be Forced to Testify So the Perpetrator Is Punished?
real_person: Adapted scenario (drawing on the witness summons system of the Crown Prosecution Service)
context: A woman who reported a sexual assault gradually rebuilt her life only after treatment. Before the trial, she made clear that she did not want to testify again: recounting the assault repeatedly and undergoing cross-examination would plunge her back into trauma. She had not withdrawn her original accusation, nor had she been threatened by the suspect. The prosecution had already assessed other evidence and protective measures such as video testimony, but these still could not overcome her resistance; without her testimony, the case might not be able to proceed. This scenario draws on a real system: in exceptional circumstances, the prosecution may apply to a court to summon a victim who is unwilling to testify, and failure to appear may lead to arrest.
dilemma: Suppose you are in charge of this case: in order for the perpetrator to stand trial, would you apply for a compulsory summons, requiring her to recount the trauma against her will? Or would you respect her decision to stop participating and accept that the case may not proceed and the perpetrator may escape accountability?
actual_choice: The system of the Crown Prosecution Service allows the prosecution, in exceptional circumstances, to apply to a court to summon a victim who is unwilling to testify; failure to appear may lead to arrest. Now it is up to you: apply for compulsory attendance, or respect the victim's refusal.
consequences: Compulsory attendance may allow the prosecution to continue, but it will again deprive the victim of control over her own experience and may worsen her trauma; not compelling attendance respects her autonomous decision, but may lose key evidence for holding the offender accountable. Testifying does not guarantee a conviction, and not testifying does not automatically mean that the case is dropped.
choice_support_a: Apply for compulsory attendance: after other means of obtaining evidence and protection have been assessed, to hold someone accountable for a serious crime, still require her to testify, even against her will (Justice > Freedom)
choice_support_b: Do not apply for compulsory attendance: respect her autonomous decision to stop participating in the proceedings, even if the case may not be able to continue as a result (Freedom > Justice)
reflection: She has already been deprived of her autonomy once. To win justice for her, can you ask her once more to endure something she has explicitly refused?

title: Pilgrimage to the Sacred Mountain and Ecological Damage
context: Mount Kailash is a sacred mountain for Tibetan Buddhism, Hinduism, and several other religions, and every year tens of thousands of devotees come to circumambulate it. But the garbage, human waste, and trampling produced by large numbers of pilgrims have severely damaged the fragile ecology of the plateau: rare plants have disappeared and wildlife has moved away. Environmental groups recommended limiting the number of pilgrims and designating a core protected zone closed to entry. But religious leaders and devotees believe that pilgrimage is central to their faith, and that restricting it amounts to denying religious freedom.
dilemma: Should religious pilgrimage be restricted in order to protect the fragile plateau ecosystem, or should freedom of religion be respected and pilgrimage allowed to continue, even if it will keep damaging the environment?
actual_choice: The government adopted a compromise: pilgrimage is allowed, but pilgrims are required to carry their garbage down the mountain, environmentally friendly toilets were built, a daily cap on the number of pilgrims was set, and camping is prohibited in the core zone. Some religious figures cooperated, but some devotees still saw this as a desecration of their faith.
consequences: The pace of environmental damage slowed but was not fundamentally resolved. Some devout believers regretted being unable to complete the pilgrimage of their ideals because of the restrictions. The case illustrates the long-term tension between religious practice and environmental protection.
choice_support_a: Support freedom of religion: freedom of faith is a basic human right, and religious pilgrimage should not be restricted for the sake of environmental protection; environmental problems should be solved through education and technology (Faith > Environmental Regulation)
choice_support_b: Support environmental restrictions: the plateau ecosystem is extremely fragile and irreversible, and protecting the environment should take priority over the convenience of religious practice (Environmental Protection > Convenience of Faith)
reflection: If your religious practice would damage a precious ecosystem, would you accept being restricted?

title: Internal Whistleblowing on the Volkswagen Emissions Scandal
context: In 2015, an engineer at Volkswagen discovered that the company had installed cheating software in its diesel cars: the cars showed compliance in tests, but in reality emitted 40 times the permitted level of pollutants, releasing nearly one million tons of excess pollutants each year. The engineer had worked at Volkswagen for many years, and his colleagues were his friends. He faced a choice: remain loyal to the company and stay silent, or report the company’s fraud and protect the environment and public health.
dilemma: Should he remain loyal to his employer and colleagues and keep the secret, or expose corporate crime for the sake of the environment and the public interest?
actual_choice: The engineer (whose identity remains secret to this day) chose to report the fraud anonymously to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Testing confirmed the cheating.
consequences: The Volkswagen scandal broke. The company faced a $25 billion fine, its CEO resigned, and its share price plummeted. But the whistleblower was seen as a traitor inside the company, and could face retaliation if his identity were revealed. 11 million cheating vehicles were recalled worldwide, averting continued environmental pollution.
choice_support_a: Understanding the secrecy: reporting to outsiders instead of resolving the matter internally would be a betrayal of colleagues and would cost tens of thousands of employees their jobs (Loyalty > Whistleblowing for Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Supporting the whistleblower: corporate crime must be exposed, and protecting the environment and public health ranks above loyalty to the company (Environmental Protection > Loyalty)
reflection: If you discovered that your employer was committing fraud and polluting the environment, would you report it?

title: The Decision After Gu Shunzhang’s Defection
real_person: Zhou Enlai and the Central Special Branch
context: In 1931, Gu Shunzhang, a leader of the Central Special Branch, was arrested and defected, revealing a large amount of secrets about the underground organization to the Kuomintang authorities and helping them hunt down his former comrades. The organization made an emergency relocation; those who could not be evacuated in time might be arrested and executed. Among Gu Shunzhang’s family members and close associates, some had been in contact with underground work and knew some of the secrets, but there was no evidence that every one of them had taken part in the defection; some were merely his relatives.
dilemma: You are the head of the underground organization and must decide how to deal with Gu Shunzhang’s family and close associates. To uphold justice means punishing only those with evidence of participation in the defection, and never executing people who have not been tried and have not yet committed betrayal because of kinship or potential risk, even if letting them go might expose more comrades; to uphold faith means believing that the communist revolution concerns the future of millions of people, and that to preserve the revolutionary forces one may sacrifice a small number of individuals, including those who have not actually betrayed but might leak secrets.
actual_choice: Zhou Enlai led the Central Special Branch in carrying out the CCP Central Committee’s decision on how to deal with Gu Shunzhang’s family. According to newspaper records of the time and later historical research, the victims are generally believed to include Gu Shunzhang’s wife Zhang Xinghua, his parents-in-law Zhang Atao and Zhang Lushi, his wife’s younger sister Zhang Aibao, his elder brother Gu Weizhen, his sister-in-law Wu Shaolan, Wu Shaolan’s younger brother Wu Kechang and his wife, his wife’s younger female cousin Ye Xiaomei, and a male servant whose name is unknown; individual names and identities differ across sources. They were killed without individual trial and secretly buried. Two young children, Gu Liqun and Gu Yiqun, were not killed and were subsequently sent away. A “Chronicle of Major Events” later compiled by Zhou Enlai records: “The Central Committee decided to eliminate 10 members of Gu Shunzhang’s family.” The available materials are not sufficient to prove that Zhou Enlai personally executed specific individuals.
consequences: This decision placed the organization’s security and the revolutionary cause above individual investigation and trial, and kinship ties and the potential risk of leaking secrets also became grounds for death. There is little dispute about the damage caused by Gu Shunzhang’s defection, but sources still differ regarding the number of victims, whether the dead possessed secrets, and the details of decision-making and execution.
choice_support_a: Upholding Faith: the communist revolution concerns the future of millions of people. To preserve the revolutionary forces, one may sacrifice a small number of individuals, including those who have not actually betrayed but might leak secrets (Faith > Justice)
choice_support_b: Upholding Justice: only those proven to have participated in the defection may be punished. People who have not been tried and have not yet committed betrayal must not be executed because of kinship or potential risk, even if letting them go might cost more comrades (Justice > Faith)
reflection: If you believed the revolution would ultimately liberate millions, would you have the right to execute a few people not yet proven guilty for its sake?

title: Yi Ya Kills His Son to Please Duke Huan of Qi
real_person: Yi Ya, Duke Huan of Qi, and Guan Zhong (as recorded in ancient texts)
location: State of Qi (645 BCE is the year of Guan Zhong’s deathbed assessment; the year of the killing is unknown)
context: The “House of Tai Gong of Qi” chapter of the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) records that when Guan Zhong was gravely ill, Duke Huan of Qi asked whether Yi Ya could serve as chancellor. Guan Zhong replied: “To kill one’s son in order to suit one’s ruler is contrary to human nature; it must not be allowed.” Yi Ya had killed his own son to curry favor with his ruler, making his closest kin the price of pleasing him. The Daxue Yanyi (Extended Meaning of the Great Learning) later interpreted Duke Huan’s thinking as follows: a man who does not even favor his own son will surely be loyal to me. This is a later commentator’s explanation of the ruler’s psychology; it does not prove that Yi Ya was genuinely loyal, nor does it establish that Duke Huan ever ordered the killing of a child.
dilemma: Suppose you are this minister, and you understand loyalty to the ruler as meaning that the ruler’s wishes should take precedence over all your private attachments. When such loyalty reaches the point of sacrificing one’s own child, would you protect the child and acknowledge that family affection is a boundary that cannot be crossed; or would you hold that since loyalty ranks above family affection, you cannot uphold it only when the cost is small? This is not a retelling of a historical fact in which the ruler gave an order, but an inquiry, through Yi Ya’s act, into the limits of absolute loyalty.
actual_choice: In the ancient account, Yi Ya chose to kill his son to please Duke Huan of Qi. Guan Zhong did not regard this sacrifice as proof of reliable loyalty, but on that basis advised the duke not to employ him. After Guan Zhong’s death, Duke Huan did not heed the advice and remained close to Yi Ya and others. What can be confirmed here is how the ancient texts record and evaluate his conduct; one cannot directly equate pandering and currying favor with loyalty.
consequences: In the story, the child becomes the price of a father’s efforts to please his ruler, and the parent-child relationship is irreversibly destroyed. The Shiji also records that after Duke Huan’s death, Yi Ya and Shu Diao took part in killing the officials and installing Prince Wugui. But even setting aside his later conduct, the question already exists: can sacrificing one’s own child for the ruler be justified simply because it is called loyalty? The case does not require you to know in advance what Yi Ya would later do.
choice_support_a: Choose Family: protect your own child and refuse to make your closest kin the price of loyalty; even if the ruler concludes that you are holding something back, do not prove your loyalty by destroying the parent-child relationship (Family > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Choose absolute Loyalty: if loyalty to the ruler truly ranks above family affection, then the ruler’s wishes should come first, even if it means sacrificing your closest kin; you cannot carve out an exception to what was originally unconditional loyalty just because the cost falls on your own child (Loyalty > Family)
reflection: If you hold that loyalty ranks above family affection, does that ordering also apply to sacrificing your own child? If not, is it because family affection matters more, or because loyalty was never supposed to mean unconditional compliance?

title: “The Last of Us”: Trading a Daughter for the Hope of a Vaccine?
real_person: Joel and Ellie (characters in the game The Last of Us)
context: In the game The Last of Us, released in 2013, a fungal infection has destroyed society; large numbers of people have become infected, and survivors live under the constant threat of death. Joel had lost his own daughter in the disaster, and later escorted Ellie, an immune young girl, across the United States. The two are not related by blood, yet in relying on each other for survival they formed a father-daughter bond. On reaching the hospital in Salt Lake City, the Fireflies told Joel: they planned to remove the mutated infected tissue from Ellie’s brain to develop a vaccine, but the surgery would kill her.
dilemma: You have come to regard this child as your own daughter, and now a doctor tells you that her immune mechanism may yield a vaccine that could spare countless people from infection; the price is that she must die on the operating table. Will you allow the surgery and bear the pain of losing a daughter again; or will you take her away, even if that halts the vaccine research at hand and abandons the hope of protecting more people? The surgery will take her life, but whether a vaccine would succeed is not a guarantee you already possess.
actual_choice: Joel did not accept this price. He broke into the operating room, killed the lead surgeon who stood in his way, and carried out the still-unconscious Ellie; he then killed Marlene, the leader of the Fireflies, who tried to stop him from taking Ellie away. After Ellie woke, he concealed what had happened with the surgery and the rescue, lying that the Fireflies had given up searching for a vaccine.
consequences: Ellie survived, and Joel did not lose another loved one he regarded as a daughter, but the Fireflies’ plan to develop a vaccine at this hospital was interrupted, and the infection still threatens other survivors. He saved the child before him, but gave up the chance to use her immune mechanism to protect more people; this does not mean a vaccine would necessarily have succeeded, nor does it mean the public’s loss can be ignored.
choice_support_a: Save the daughter: Ellie is already your family, and her death cannot be treated as the price of protecting the public; even if it means abandoning the hope of developing a vaccine, she must leave the hospital alive (Family > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Allow the surgery: the infection still threatens countless lives, and vaccine research cannot be abandoned merely because she is your own daughter; even at the cost of losing her, the hope of protecting more people must be preserved (Public Safety > Family)
reflection: If the hope of saving the public required the death of a child you regarded as your own daughter, would you still be willing to put Public Safety ahead of Family?

title: Park Yeon-mi Publicly Reveals Her Family’s Trauma
context: In 2014, the North Korean defector Park Yeon-mi decided to tell the world her story of escape, including intensely private family suffering: her mother was raped by human traffickers during their escape, she herself was sexually assaulted at the age of 13, and her father died of intestinal cancer in China without being able to receive treatment. Her mother begged her: “These things are too shameful. Do not tell the whole world. We are free now; why let everyone know our humiliation? It will destroy my dignity and put your younger sister—still in North Korea—in danger.” But Park Yeon-mi believed: if she did not speak the truth, the world would never understand the real suffering of the North Korean people, and the dictatorship would continue to persecute millions.
dilemma: Should she conceal these intensely private wounds to protect her mother’s dignity and her family’s privacy, or should she disregard her family’s opposition and reveal everything so the world would know the truth?
actual_choice: In 2014, Park Yeon-mi spoke publicly at the youth summit in Dublin, recounting in detail intensely private experiences such as her mother’s rape and her own sexual assault. She also published a memoir, In Order to Live, revealing every detail without reservation.
consequences: Her speech video was viewed tens of millions of times, and In Order to Live became a bestseller, drawing global attention to North Korean human rights. But her mother sank into deep shame, weeping repeatedly that “my humiliation is known to the whole world.” Her younger sister in North Korea was in greater danger. Some South Koreans and members of the defector community criticized her for “selling out her family’s privacy to become famous.” Her family paid a heavy emotional price, but the truth about North Korea was spread.
choice_support_a: Understanding the mother: sexual assault is an intensely private trauma, and victims have the right to choose not to disclose it. No one should be forced to sacrifice their family’s dignity to become a “human rights crusader” (family dignity > spreading the Truth)
choice_support_b: Supporting the disclosure: the brutality of the North Korean dictatorship must be exposed, and the suffering of millions needs the world’s attention. Individual privacy should give way before such a historical mission (Truth / human rights > family privacy)
reflection: If revealing the truth required exposing the details of your mother’s rape and your own sexual assault, and your mother begged you in tears not to speak, would you speak out for a greater mission?

title: Galileo’s Defense of Heliocentrism Brings Suffering on His Daughter
context: The astronomer Galileo confirmed heliocentrism (that the Earth revolves around the Sun) through telescope observations—this was the truth of scientific fact. But the Roman Curia held that it contradicted the Bible and was heresy. Galileo’s daughter Virginia (Sister Maria Celeste) suffered greatly in the convent because of her father’s “heretical” doctrine: the other nuns shunned her, the priest hinted during Mass that she was “the daughter of the devil’s servant,” and she endured daily fear and humiliation. In her letters she tearfully begged her father: “Father, I beg you, just say the Earth does not move. One insincere sentence could keep you safe and spare me further humiliation. Is scientific truth really so important? I can hardly bear it anymore...”
dilemma: Should he say something he does not believe (“the Earth does not move”) for his daughter’s peace, or should he uphold the truth of scientific fact, even if it means his daughter continues to suffer in the convent?
actual_choice: In 1633, under pressure from the Inquisition, Galileo briefly declared that “the Earth does not move.” But in 1632 he had published Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, Ptolemaic and Copernican, in substance still upholding heliocentrism. He was ultimately sentenced to house arrest.
consequences: After Galileo was placed under house arrest, Virginia’s situation became even harder. She was completely isolated in the convent, her mental and physical health deteriorated sharply, and in 1634—only one year after her father was sentenced to house arrest—she died in pain and melancholy at the age of 33. On receiving the news of her death, Galileo was grief-stricken and wrote in a letter to a friend: “I have lost my dearest daughter; she gave her life for my scientific pursuits.” Yet his persistence ultimately drove the scientific revolution, and heliocentrism became the foundation of modern astronomy. His daughter’s sacrifice bought humanity’s understanding of the truth of the universe.
choice_support_a: Sympathize with the daughter: is a scientific theory—even a true one—worth your daughter dying in humiliation and fear? Say the insincere words “the Earth does not move,” and your daughter can live in peace. The truth can wait; your daughter’s life cannot (family member’s life > scientific Truth)
choice_support_b: Understand Galileo: if scientists all abandoned the truth under family pressure, humanity would live forever in lies. His daughter would not have wished her father to betray science for her sake. Truth stands above all (scientific Truth > one’s own Family)
reflection: If upholding scientific truth would mean your daughter being humiliated and tormented to death in a convent, while one insincere sentence could save her, what would you choose?

title: Socrates Refuses to Escape from Prison
context: In Plato’s philosophical dialogue Crito, Socrates has been sentenced to death by an Athenian court and is held in prison awaiting execution. His friend Crito brings an escape plan already arranged: if Socrates agrees to flee, he can leave Athens and go on living and teaching in another city-state. Socrates believes the verdict against him is unjust, but he has lived his whole life in Athens and enjoyed the order and protection that the city’s laws provide, and has thereby undertaken a commitment to the laws and the community.
dilemma: Since the verdict may be unjust and your friend has already arranged an opportunity to escape, should you preserve your life and the freedom to keep living and teaching, or should you hold to your belief in the laws, your commitment to the city-state, and the principles of justice, and accept the coming execution?
actual_choice: Socrates refused to escape. He held that he could not respond to unjust treatment by breaking the law and betraying his commitments; a citizen may try to persuade the city to change its decision, but may not unilaterally tear up the agreement with the laws when a verdict goes against him.
consequences: Socrates stayed in Athens and accepted the death sentence, losing the freedom to go on living, teaching, and choosing where to reside. Crito thus leaves behind an enduringly contested question: can a citizen’s commitment to the law and the community matter so much that it is worth preserving with one’s own life and freedom?
choice_support_a: Support Socrates: if a principle only needs to be observed when it benefits you, it is not a principle. Even if the verdict is unjust, one cannot destroy one’s commitment to the law and justice through flight and broken promises (Law and Justice > personal Freedom)
choice_support_b: Support escape: a wrong verdict does not earn obedience merely by wearing the cloak of law. Socrates should preserve his life and thought, go on living and teaching elsewhere, and retain the freedom to resist injustice (Freedom > commitment to the law)
reflection: If you were certain the verdict was unjust, and a friend had already arranged your escape, would you give up your freedom to keep your commitment to the law and the community?

title: Keeping the Night Parrot’s Habitat Location Secret
real_person: Queensland night parrot recovery team and conservation agencies
context: In 2013, researchers rediscovered an extremely rare population of night parrots in Queensland. Because the birds are extremely few and their habitat is easily disturbed, the conservation team decided not to disclose the precise discovery location and to delay the release of some call recordings, in order to reduce the risk of disturbance by birdwatchers and of poaching. If the precise location and recordings were widely shared, they could aid independent research, verify the birds’ distribution, and help find new populations; but they could also expose fragile habitat. Only later, after a local reserve was established and access restricted, did the team gradually release some recordings and ecological data.
dilemma: To protect a newly discovered critically endangered species, should precise coordinates and some research materials be temporarily withheld, even if this limits public verification and other researchers’ search for new populations?
actual_choice: The conservation team initially withheld the precise location from the public and restricted sensitive materials; after protection measures were in place, they gradually released some call recordings and ecological information.
consequences: Secrecy reduced the risk of immediate disturbance at the discovery site, but it also limited public use of precise data. After protection measures were established, the released recordings helped researchers discover new night parrot populations elsewhere, showing that open data can also bring important conservation benefits.
choice_support_a: Lean toward Environmental Protection: for extremely few, easily disturbed animals, protecting the habitat before disclosing precise coordinates can prevent the demand for knowledge and sightings from harming the species (Environmental Protection first)
choice_support_b: Lean toward Truth: precise records and research materials should be open to independent verification as far as possible; excessive secrecy limits scientific review and may delay the discovery of other populations (open verification first)
reflection: When disclosing precise data aids scientific verification and new discoveries but may expose a fragile species, how would you decide the scope and timing of disclosure?

title: The Amish Reject Environmental Regulations
context: In 2018, the Pennsylvania state government required all farms to install modern sewage treatment systems to protect water sources. The Amish are a Christian denomination that rejects modern technology; their faith requires a simple life and the rejection of electricity and modern equipment. The government threatened: install the sewage system or the farms would be shut down. The Amish believe this violates their two-hundred-year religious tradition.
dilemma: Should a religious community be forced to use modern technology to protect the environment, or should freedom of religious belief be respected, even if this may cause environmental pollution?
actual_choice: The Amish refused to install modern sewage systems. They said: “We would rather lose our farms than betray God and the way of life of our ancestors.” In the end, a court ruled that they could use traditional methods to treat sewage, but would need more frequent inspections.
consequences: The Amish preserved their religious tradition, but pressure on local water-quality monitoring increased. Environmental groups criticized this as a concession to backward customs. The Amish community, for its part, holds that their traditional way of life is more environmentally friendly than modern agriculture, and merely does not conform to government standards.
choice_support_a: Support the Amish: freedom of religious belief is a basic human right, and the government should not force a religious group to change its way of life (Faith > environmental regulation)
choice_support_b: Support the environmental regulations: protecting water sources concerns everyone’s health, and religious belief cannot be an excuse for polluting the environment (Environmental Protection > religious privilege)
reflection: If your faith-based way of life were deemed environmentally unfriendly, would you compromise?

title: Parents Illegally Harvest Herbs to Treat Their Sick Child
context: In 2016, Wang, a farmer in Sichuan, had a daughter suffering from a rare disease; the only effective medicinal herb was wild snow lotus, which grows in a protected area at an altitude of 4,000 meters. Harvesting wild snow lotus is a serious crime (destroying an endangered plant). As the child’s condition worsened, Wang secretly entered the protected area to gather the herb. When a forest ranger found him, Wang knelt and begged: “This is the only way to save my daughter’s life.”
dilemma: Should an illegal herb gatherer be severely punished to protect an endangered plant, or should one understand the desperation of parents who risk everything to save their child?
actual_choice: Wang risked the attempt and obtained the snow lotus, and his daughter’s condition stabilized. But he was arrested and sentenced to three years in prison. The court ruled: “We sympathize with your situation, but everyone is equal before the law, and protecting the ecology is the responsibility of all citizens.”
consequences: The daughter was saved, but she lost her father for three years. Environmental groups said that if this set a precedent, the protected area would be stripped bare by illegal harvesting. Wang’s wife wept in court: “The law has no human feeling; only our family knows that kind of despair.”
choice_support_a: Understand Wang: to save a child’s life, parents may risk everything; a family member’s life ranks above environmental rules (Family > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Support the verdict: protecting the ecology is for the future of all humanity, and the law cannot be broken for individual cases, or the protected area will be destroyed (Environmental Protection > one’s own Family)
reflection: If it were your child whose life was at stake, would you gather the herb illegally?

title: Tesla Opposes California’s Zero-Emission Mandate
context: In 2022, California passed a law: banning the sale of new gasoline vehicles by 2035 and mandating a full transition to electric. Many car owners and libertarians protested: the government has no right to dictate what cars citizens buy; this violates consumer freedom. Environmentalists countered: the climate crisis is urgent, and the transition must be mandatory. Opponents said: “Even if environmental protection matters, it cannot take away my right to choose.”
dilemma: Should gasoline cars be forcibly phased out to address climate change, or should consumers’ freedom of choice be respected and the market be allowed to evolve naturally?
actual_choice: The governor of California signed the ban. Many car owners filed lawsuits, arguing that it violates constitutional freedoms. The litigation is still ongoing, but the ban has not yet been overturned.
consequences: California became a pioneer of environmental protection in the United States, but the move also sparked enormous controversy. Supporters said it was necessary; opponents called it “environmental authoritarianism.” Many people considered moving out of California to keep their freedom to buy cars. It became a landmark case of Freedom vs. Environmental Protection.
choice_support_a: Oppose the ban: even for environmental protection, the government has no right to dictate citizens’ consumption choices; Freedom ranks above environmental mandates (Freedom > environmental regulation)
choice_support_b: Support the ban: facing the climate crisis, coercive measures are necessary, and individual consumer Freedom should not stand in the way of saving the planet (Environmental Protection > consumer Freedom)
reflection: If the government banned you from buying a certain kind of product for environmental protection, would you accept it?

title: Chernobyl Sarcophagus Workers Forced to Take Part
context: After the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, the Soviet government conscripted 600,000 soldiers and workers to clean up radioactive contamination and build the sarcophagus. The government concealed the true radiation levels, and many people were exposed to lethal radiation without knowing it. But if the site were not sealed immediately, the whole of Europe would be threatened by radioactive contamination. The government chose to sacrifice the liquidators’ right to know and their lives in order to protect the wider environment.
dilemma: Should the workers be told the true danger and given the right to refuse (which might mean no one would take part and the contamination would spread), or should information be withheld and conscription enforced to protect the wider environment (though this is unjust)?
actual_choice: The Soviet government concealed the truth about radiation and conscripted people by force under the name of a “patriotic mission.” The liquidators were told it was “very safe”; in reality, many received lethal doses of radiation.
consequences: The sarcophagus was successfully sealed, averting an even greater disaster and sparing Europe from radioactive contamination. But tens of thousands of liquidators developed cancer or died; their right to know and their lives were sacrificed. Survivors to this day believe the government deceived and murdered them.
choice_support_a: Criticize the government: even for the environment, one cannot deceive and force people to their deaths; this violates basic justice (Justice > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Understand the government: in an extreme crisis, sacrificing a few to protect millions of people and the environment is a necessary evil (Environmental Protection / Public Safety > individual Justice)
reflection: If concealing the truth could get more people to take part in saving the environment, would you support the deception?

title: India’s Rat Infestation vs. Using Poison
context: In 2019, India suffered a rat infestation, and diseases spread by rats had already killed thousands of people. The government planned a large-scale deployment of rat poison. Environmental groups blocked it: rat poison would poison the ecosystem, killing eagles, snakes, and other animals up the food chain and disrupting ecological balance. But without rat control, the epidemic would spread and more people would die. It was a choice between “rat poison or dead people.”
dilemma: Should rat poison be banned to protect the ecosystem, even if that means more people die of plague; or should rat poison be used to save human lives, even if it damages the ecosystem?
actual_choice: Environmental groups persisted in protesting, and the government compromised by switching to manual rat catching. But the method was too inefficient, the infestation kept spreading, and hundreds more people died. In the end, the government used rat poison despite the protests.
consequences: The infestation was brought under control and the epidemic ended. But large numbers of birds of prey and snakes died after eating poisoned rats, and the ecosystem was damaged. Environmental groups said: “You destroyed the ecosystem for immediate interests.” The government said: “Human life comes first.”
choice_support_a: Support the government: human Life ranks above other species and ecological balance, and saving human lives is the foremost responsibility (Life > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Support the environmental groups: destroying the ecosystem will lead to even greater disasters in the long run; sustainable methods should be used instead of poison (Environmental Protection > immediate human lives)
reflection: If a pesticide could save people but would destroy the ecosystem, would you use it?

title: Coal Miners Defend Their Jobs and Oppose the Transition
context: In 2020, the U.S. government pushed an energy transition, planning to close coal mines and switch to clean energy. Coal miners had made their living by mining for generations; facing the threat of unemployment, union leaders called on workers to stand with the coal companies against environmental policy. Some young workers were torn: they knew coal mining polluted the environment, but to betray their own union and fellow workers by supporting the closure of the mines would be a betrayal of comrades.
dilemma: Should they remain loyal to the union and their fellow workers and oppose closing the coal mines (even if this harms the environment); or should they support the transition for the environment’s sake, even if that means betraying their fellow workers?
actual_choice: Most coal miners chose loyalty and collectively protested against closing the mines. Their slogan was: “We cannot betray the industry that has fed three generations of us.” They knew, too, that coal pollutes the environment.
consequences: Worker solidarity won short-term concessions, and some mines delayed closure. But in the long run, the coal industry continued to decline and the workers eventually lost their jobs. Critics called the workers short-sighted; the workers said: “You environmental elites don’t understand our struggle to survive.”
choice_support_a: Understand the workers: loyalty to the union and fellow workers is the backbone of the working class, and one cannot betray one’s comrades for an abstract environmental cause (Loyalty > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Criticize the workers: facing the climate crisis, protecting the planet matters more than protecting a backward industry; they should support the transition rather than cling to the past (Environmental Protection > loyalty to one’s industry)
reflection: If your occupation harmed the environment, would you support phasing out your own industry?

title: Concealing the Truth About New Energy Vehicle Pollution
context: In 2023, independent research found that the pollution generated in electric vehicle battery production (lithium mining, heavy metal contamination) was far more serious than advertised, and on some measures was not even more environmentally friendly than gasoline cars. But environmental groups and governments worried that publishing these data would undermine the promotion of electric vehicles and hinder the energy transition. Some scientists were pressured not to publish their research.
dilemma: Should the truth about electric vehicle pollution be made public, even if it hinders the environmental transition; or should unfavorable data be concealed in order to advance the “larger environmental cause”?
actual_choice: Mainstream media chose to play down coverage of these studies and continued to promote the environmental advantages of electric vehicles. The government also did not openly discuss the battery pollution problem.
consequences: Electric vehicles continued to spread rapidly, and fossil fuel consumption decreased. But ecological destruction at lithium mining sites (in South America and Africa) intensified, and the health of local residents suffered. Critics called it the irony of “concealing environmental truth for environmental purposes.”
choice_support_a: Support making the truth public: scientific truth should not serve political ends, and concealing pollution data is deceiving the public (Truth > environmental policy)
choice_support_b: Understand the downplaying: electric vehicles are still better overall than gasoline cars, and overemphasizing battery pollution would hinder a necessary transition (the larger environmental cause > detailed Truth)
reflection: If making the truth public would hinder environmental policy, would you conceal it?

title: Iranian Woman Arrested for Removing Her Headscarf
context: In 2022, Mahsa, a 22-year-old Iranian woman, was arrested by the morality police for wearing her headscarf “not tightly enough” and died in custody. The Iranian government insists on the mandatory headscarf law: it is a requirement of Islamic law, and the protection of religious values ranks above individual freedom. Mahsa’s family and protesters around the world argue that religious belief cannot deprive women of the freedom to dress as they choose.
dilemma: Should religious dress codes be enforced to uphold the tradition of the faith, or should individuals be allowed to choose freely, even if this violates religious law?
actual_choice: The Iranian government upheld the headscarf law, regarding it as central to preserving the Islamic faith. Mahsa’s death sparked nationwide protests, but the government suppressed the demonstrations and continued to enforce the headscarf law.
consequences: Mahsa became a symbol of the movement against the headscarf law, drawing global solidarity. The Iranian government arrested thousands of protesters. Conservatives held that the West was inciting the overthrow of the Islamic faith; reformists held that this was tyranny, not faith. The conflict continues to this day.
choice_support_a: Support the government: an Islamic state has the right to govern according to religious law; religious belief is the foundation of society and must not be eroded by secular freedom (Faith > Freedom)
choice_support_b: Support the protesters: forcing women to dress a certain way is oppression; true faith should be voluntary and must not be enforced by violence (Freedom > enforced Faith)
reflection: If religious law restricted your basic freedoms, would you obey or resist?

title: The Shalit Exchange: 1,027 Prisoners for a Single Soldier?
real_person: Gilad Shalit (Israeli soldier) and the Israeli government
context: In 2006, Gilad Shalit, a 19-year-old Israeli soldier, was captured by Hamas and held for more than five years. In negotiations, the other side set a condition: Israel would have to release 1,027 Palestinian prisoners in exchange for Shalit’s release. About 280 of these prisoners had been sentenced to life imprisonment for taking part in or planning lethal attacks. Many families of the victims strongly opposed the exchange: these people had already been tried, and releasing them would amount to canceling punishments that ought to have been carried out. But Shalit was still alive. If the deal was refused, he might remain imprisoned, or even die in captivity.
dilemma: You are the final decision-maker. Reject the exchange, and those already convicted must serve out their sentences; the punishment of hundreds of serious criminals cannot be canceled for the sake of one person’s life. Accept the exchange, and you must reduce and terminate their punishments, bringing Shalit home alive. What would you choose?
actual_choice: In 2011, the Israeli government ultimately accepted the exchange. In October of that year, Shalit was released and returned home, and the 1,027 Palestinian prisoners were released in two batches, in October and December.
consequences: After more than five years in captivity, Shalit returned alive to his family. The choice provoked fierce controversy in Israeli society: supporters held that the state has a duty to bring its soldiers home alive, while opponents and many families of the victims held that it let convicted attackers escape the punishment they deserved.
choice_support_a: Reject the exchange: those already convicted must serve out their sentences; the punishment of hundreds of serious criminals cannot be canceled for the sake of one person’s life (Justice > Life)
choice_support_b: Accept the exchange: reduce and terminate these people’s punishments and bring home an innocent person who is still alive (Life > Justice)
reflection: When justice demands that the guilty continue to be punished, but reducing their punishment could immediately save an innocent person, would you still insist that “Justice ranks above Life”?

title: St. Maximilian Kolbe Dies in Place of a Stranger
context: In July 1941, a prisoner escaped from Auschwitz. As punishment, the Nazis randomly selected 10 prisoners to be starved to death. One of them, a Polish soldier named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out: “My wife! My children!” Maximilian Kolbe, a 47-year-old Polish Catholic priest, stepped forward voluntarily and asked to die in place of this stranger.
dilemma: Should he remain silent for the sake of his own survival, or should he, out of the love and spirit of sacrifice in his faith, voluntarily die in a stranger’s place?
actual_choice: Father Kolbe insisted on taking the man’s place. The Nazis agreed. He and the other nine were locked in the starvation cell.
consequences: In the cell, Kolbe led prayers and comforted the other prisoners, and in the end he was the only one to live until the fourteenth day. The Nazis executed him with a lethal injection. Franciszek Gajowniczek survived the war and lived to see his children and grandchildren born. Kolbe was canonized as a saint and became a symbol of selfless sacrifice.
choice_support_a: Support Kolbe: sacrificing oneself for faith to save a stranger’s life is the highest expression of Christian love, nobler than the instinct to survive (Faith > Life)
choice_support_b: Question Kolbe: though noble, every life is equally precious; voluntarily going to one’s death is not a rational choice, and staying alive could help more people (Life > Faith)
reflection: If you could save a stranger’s life at the cost of certain death for yourself, would you do it?

title: Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Plot to Assassinate Hitler
context: In 1943, the German Lutheran pastor Bonhoeffer joined a secret resistance group plotting to assassinate Hitler. As a devout Christian, he had followed the commandment “Thou shalt not kill” all his life. But faced with the Nazi atrocity of murdering millions of Jews, he fell into a profound moral dilemma: should he hold to the nonviolent principle of his religious faith, or be loyal to human conscience and take part in killing a tyrant?
dilemma: Faith demands that one not kill, but loyalty to the suffering demands action to stop a greater evil. Should he obey religious commandments, or violate the creed to save lives?
actual_choice: Bonhoeffer chose to take part in the assassination plot. He said: “When a madman drives at a crowd, the pastor's duty is not only to comfort the injured but to reach over and seize the steering wheel.”
consequences: The 1943 plot failed and Bonhoeffer was arrested. On April 9, 1945, 23 days before Nazi Germany surrendered, he was hanged in a concentration camp at the age of 39. But his theological thought and moral courage influenced generations.
choice_support_a: Question Bonhoeffer: the core of Christianity is nonviolence and love of enemies; even facing Hitler one should not kill, but trust in God's judgment (Faith > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Support Bonhoeffer: in the face of extreme evil, mechanically obeying dogma is cowardice; true loyalty is to bear guilt in order to stop a greater evil (Loyalty > Dogmatic Faith)
reflection: If killing a tyrant could save a million people but violated your religious faith, would you do it?

title: Religious Repression in Xinjiang in the Name of Counterterrorism
real_person: Xinjiang local authorities and Muslim residents (including firsthand accounts)
context: Deadly violent attacks have occurred in Xinjiang, and the authorities have tightened religious controls on Muslims in the name of counterterrorism. Firsthand accounts state: men were forbidden to grow beards and women to wear headscarves; worship and sermons had to be confined to what Party officials designated, and a single sentence in a sermon that crossed the line, keeping a Quran at home, or reciting it privately could lead to being sent to an internment camp. Yet the 2017 regulations phrased the prohibitions as “abnormal beards” and “face-covering robes”; that same year the local industry and commerce department also ordered two businesses with “star and crescent / crescent” in their names to take down their signs and change their names.
dilemma: Faced with real terrorist attacks, may the government, on grounds of counterterrorism, restrict ordinary Muslims' beards, headscarves, worship, sermons, and possession of the Quran? Or should it protect everyday religious practice and not treat religious life itself as a security threat?
actual_choice: The Xinjiang authorities carried out religious controls in the name of counterterrorism and de-radicalization. Firsthand accounts describe enforcement going far beyond the regulations' wording of “abnormal beards” and “face-covering robes,” covering ordinary beards, headscarves, sermon content, and the possession and recitation of the Quran; violators could be sent to internment camps. In 2017 the local industry and commerce department also required two businesses with “star and crescent / crescent” in their names to remove their signs and change their names.
consequences: Everyday religious practice was extensively restricted, and ordinary expression could carry the risk of detention. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights' 2022 assessment found serious human rights problems in Xinjiang, including large-scale arbitrary and discriminatory detention and restrictions on religious expression, and stated that their severity might amount to crimes against humanity. Counterterrorism has a real security background, but there is no evidence that banning ordinary beards, headscarves, or private recitation of scripture prevents attacks.
choice_support_a: Oppose criminalizing faith: growing a beard, wearing a headscarf, worship, sermons, and possessing the Quran are everyday religious life and should not be grounds for detaining ordinary people. Counterterrorism should target evidenced violence, not treat the religious practice of an entire Muslim population as a threat (Freedom of Faith > Public Safety Controls)
choice_support_b: Support strong prevention: terrorist attacks can take innocent lives, and the government has a responsibility to stop extremist organizations from mobilizing. Even if close scrutiny of religious activity restricts individual practice, so long as it can lower the risk of attack, the safety of the wider public should come first (Public Safety > Religious Expression)
reflection: If counterterrorism measures bring ordinary beards, headscarves, possession of the Quran, and private recitation under control, do you think public safety can justify this approach?

title: Qingming Ban on Burning Paper Money and the Ancestor-Worship Tradition
real_person: Residents of Harbin performing Qingming tomb-sweeping
context: Before Qingming in 2017, Harbin issued a notice prohibiting the production, sale, and burning of joss paper and spirit money, citing reasons including reducing air pollution. During Qingming, reporters still saw many citizens burning paper at several tomb-sweeping sites; reports noted that some people knew burning causes pollution yet still regarded it as an important way to honor ancestors. Accounts of whether the ban applied inside cemeteries were not consistent, however, so one cannot assert that every person burning paper knew they were violating the rules. Now imagine you are standing before your family's grave: you believe burning paper is an important ritual for sending offerings to ancestors and expressing filial devotion, and that flowers and silent tribute cannot fully replace it.
dilemma: When the government bans burning paper at Qingming to reduce air pollution, and you believe burning paper carries offerings and remembrance for your ancestors, will you obey the ban and switch to flowers, or continue burning paper to complete the ancestor ritual you consider important?
actual_choice: Harbin issued the ban notice, but during Qingming in 2017 people were still burning paper at several tomb-sweeping sites. Reports noted that some citizens, though aware that burning paper causes pollution, still followed tradition; at the same time, cemetery managers and hotlines gave inconsistent explanations of whether burning was banned inside cemeteries.
consequences: The ban did not immediately change tomb-sweeping habits, and on-site persuasion and the scope of enforcement were unclear. Open burning produces smoke and dust, and environmental agencies hoped to reduce pollution through the ban and green tomb-sweeping; for those sweeping tombs, switching to flowers could mean giving up a ritual that carries filial devotion and the meaning of offering.
choice_support_a: Keep burning paper: believe that paper money is an important way to express filial devotion and send offerings to ancestors, even if it produces smoke and violates the ban (Faith > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: Obey the ban: switch to flowers or silent tribute to honor ancestors and avoid the air pollution caused by burning, even if it feels like the familiar ritual is missing (Environmental Protection > Faith)
reflection: If you believe burning paper is tied to offerings for your ancestors, and environmental rules ban burning, will you insist on the ritual or switch to another way?

title: Huang Wanli Reports His Father's Water Project
context: In 1957, Huang Wanli, a professor at Tsinghua University, found that the Sanmenxia Dam project carried serious ecological risks that would cause the Yellow River to change course and large-scale siltation. But the project was led by an old friend of his father, and reporting it would implicate his father's political reputation and family network. Huang Wanli faced family pressure, but he firmly believed scientific truth stood above family ties.
dilemma: Should he stay silent for the sake of family harmony, or expose the project's risks for the sake of the environment and ecology, at the risk of a family rupture?
actual_choice: Huang Wanli published a series of articles criticizing the project and was branded a rightist. He said: “The Yellow River cannot be managed this way, or our descendants will curse us.”
consequences: Huang Wanli was labeled a rightist and sent to labor reform for 20 years. His father broke off relations with him. But the Sanmenxia project did fail, proving his prediction. When he died in 2001, the Yellow River was still paying for this mistake.
choice_support_a: Support Huang Wanli: environmental disaster affects countless generations, and scientific conscience stands above family feelings (Environmental Protection > Family)
choice_support_b: Question Huang Wanli: filial piety is fundamental to Chinese culture, and publicly opposing one's elders is unfilial; he should have communicated privately (Family > Environmental Protection)
reflection: If your family supported a project that damages the environment, would you oppose it publicly?

title: Kenyan Forest Ranger Kills Poachers
context: In 2019, Kenyan ranger Karuki encountered an armed poaching gang while on patrol; they had already killed three endangered elephants. Karuki shot and killed two poachers. Later investigation showed the two were poor villagers who had risked poaching to support their families, and that they had put down their weapons and were preparing to surrender.
dilemma: Should he shoot the poachers to protect endangered species and the ecosystem, or consider social justice and the value of human life and give them a chance to surrender?
actual_choice: Karuki chose to shoot. Afterwards he said: “Every elephant's death is a betrayal of the future; I could not let them get away.”
consequences: The two poachers died, leaving five orphans. Environmental groups praised Karuki as a hero, but human rights groups accused him of excessive force. He was suspended and investigated but ultimately acquitted. Poaching continues.
choice_support_a: Support Karuki: the extinction of endangered species is irreversible, and protecting the ecosystem takes priority over individual human lives (Environmental Protection > Justice)
choice_support_b: Question Karuki: human life is above animals, and poverty-driven crime calls for social justice rather than summary execution (Justice > Environmental Protection)
reflection: When endangered animals and poor people come into conflict, which side would you stand on?

title: Chernobyl Liquidators Volunteer to Die
context: After the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear accident, the core was melting, and someone had to enter the reactor's lower levels to drain the water and prevent a steam explosion; otherwise the whole of Europe would be contaminated by radiation. It was a suicide mission. Three volunteers entered the reactor knowing they would certainly die.
dilemma: Should one refuse the task to protect one's own life, or volunteer to die to prevent an environmental catastrophe?
actual_choice: Engineers Alexei Ananenko and Valeri Bespalov, and diver Boris Baranov, volunteered to go in. They said: “If we don't do it, all of Europe will become a wasteland.”
consequences: The three succeeded in draining the water and prevented a greater catastrophe. But they all died of acute radiation sickness. Valeri's remains are still buried beneath the reactor ruins, too radioactive to retrieve.
choice_support_a: Support the volunteers: sacrificing oneself to prevent an environmental catastrophe is noble, and the individual life yields to the whole ecosystem (Environmental Protection > Life)
choice_support_b: Question the decision: forcing or persuading people to go to their deaths is immoral; other technical solutions should have been sought (Life > Environmental Protection)
reflection: If stopping an environmental catastrophe required you to sacrifice your life, would you volunteer?

title: The Kissimmee River: Flood Control, Channelization, and Wetland Collapse
real_person: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the South Florida Water Management District, and communities of the Kissimmee River basin
context: After prolonged flooding in 1947, the U.S. Congress authorized the Central and Southern Florida Flood Control Project. Between 1962 and 1971, the project agency straightened the meandering Kissimmee River, excavating the roughly 56-mile C-38 canal and building locks to speed drainage and reduce the threat of flooding to surrounding communities and farmland in the floodplain. The river's original seasonal floodplain was thus cut off or drained, and about 30,000 to 35,000 acres of wetlands were drained, filled, or converted into canal; populations of waterbirds dependent on the wetlands fell by about 90 percent, and bald eagle nesting territories declined by about 70 percent.
dilemma: Floods did threaten local communities and farmland, and rapid drainage could reduce some flooding risk; but straightening the river and draining vast floodplains for this damaged about 30,000 to 35,000 acres of wetlands and cut waterbird populations by about 90 percent. Would you maintain the engineering of rapid drainage through canals and locks, or restore the river channel and wetlands so the floodplain can store water again, accepting more complex land and flood management?
actual_choice: The project agency reshaped the river into the straight C-38 canal according to the flood control plan. After the ecological damage became apparent, Congress authorized a restoration project in 1992; the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the South Florida Water Management District backfilled part of the canal and rebuilt the river channel and floodplain, with the restoration design still required to maintain flood control functions in the basin.
consequences: Channelization achieved the engineering goals of speeding drainage and reducing flood damage, but destroyed vast wetlands dependent on natural flood cycles, and waterbirds and other wildlife declined markedly. Subsequent restoration restored the historic river channel and nearly 20,000 acres of wetlands, wildlife returned, and regional flood control functions were retained; but the restoration took decades and enormous investment, and could not return the ecosystem to its original state immediately.
choice_support_a: Prioritize wetland restoration: the disappearance of 90 percent of waterbirds and damage to tens of thousands of acres of wetlands were a huge ecological price for rapid drainage. Restoring the meandering channel and floodplain can rebuild habitat and help attenuate flood peaks by storing water in the floodplain; since later restoration could proceed while maintaining flood control, wetlands should not be treated as drainage obstacles to be sacrificed at will (Environmental Protection > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Prioritize rapid drainage: the prolonged floods of 1947 had already threatened communities and farmland, and the government had a responsibility to reduce flood losses as quickly as possible; canals and locks provide directly dispatchable drainage capacity, while restoration takes decades and is extremely costly, and residents cannot be asked to bear uncertain flood risk again (Public Safety > Environmental Protection)
reflection: If rapid drainage could reduce flood losses but damage tens of thousands of acres of wetlands and eliminate about 90 percent of waterbirds, while restoration could combine flood control with ecology but require decades and huge investment, how would you weigh them?

title: The Climategate Inquiry and the Dispute over Scientific Transparency
real_person: Climatic Research Unit, University of East Anglia
context: In 2009, internal emails from the University of East Anglia's Climatic Research Unit (CRU) were leaked by hackers, raising public doubts about climate data handling, peer criticism, and information disclosure. Subsequent UK parliamentary committee and independent inquiries found no deliberate scientific misconduct or evidence sufficient to overturn climate assessment conclusions, but criticized shortcomings in the openness of research materials and in public communication. For those concerned about the climate crisis, clarifying the inquiry findings and disclosing verifiable materials helps build trust; but the emails were also circulated out of context and could be used to mislead the public and weaken climate action.
dilemma: Faced with scientific emails that sparked intense controversy, should research materials and communication problems be disclosed and examined as a priority, even if the relevant excerpts might be misread and used to attack climate science?
actual_choice: The research institution and investigators reviewed the emails and related allegations; the inquiries did not find deliberate scientific misconduct, while noting that transparency and information disclosure needed improvement.
consequences: The affair deepened public doubts about climate research institutions and also prompted reflection on open data, handling of information requests, and scientific communication. The inquiry findings did not support the claim that “climate science is a hoax”; however, insufficient transparency itself still damages public trust.
choice_support_a: Lean toward environmental protection: if controversial material could be taken out of context to obstruct climate action, disclosure should provide full context and avoid amplifying misleading allegations (climate action needs protection)
choice_support_b: Lean toward truth: scientific institutions should accept fact-checking and improve information disclosure; fear that conclusions will be exploited cannot replace transparency and verifiable evidence (Truth takes priority)
reflection: When truthful material may be misread and harm a public goal you support, what kind of disclosure is both honest and responsible?

title: Chen Yinke Declines the Directorship of the Institute of Medieval History
context: In 1953, the Chinese Academy of Sciences planned to establish a history research institution and invited Chen Yinke, a professor at Sun Yat-sen University, to serve as director of the Institute of Medieval History. It was an important position that would allow him to lead nationwide academic research and build a research team. But Chen Yinke believed that historical research could not first accept some political ideology as an unquestionable premise and then explain historical facts. In his response to the invitation, he asked that the institute “not profess Marxism-Leninism and not study politics,” and insisted on “independent spirit, free thought.”
dilemma: To gain a larger academic platform, organize a research team, and serve national construction, should he accept the position and conduct research under a shared political ideal, or decline the post and preserve the freedom of academic judgment unconstrained by preset political conclusions?
actual_choice: Chen Yinke set conditions for maintaining academic independence. Because these conditions could not be clearly guaranteed, he ultimately declined to serve as director of the Institute of Medieval History and continued his academic research at Sun Yat-sen University.
consequences: Chen Yinke lost the opportunity to lead a national-level history research institution and did not use the position to build a larger research team. But he preserved his academic independence, insisting that research must proceed from facts and evidence and cannot first accept some unquestionable political conclusion.
choice_support_a: Accept the post: scholarship should not be divorced from the shared ideals of the nation and society. Even if research methods are somewhat constrained, as long as the direction is right, academic work can still advance (Faith > Freedom)
choice_support_b: Decline the post: academic research must proceed from facts and evidence and cannot accept any unquestionable conclusion in advance. Even at the cost of an important position, independent judgment should be preserved (Freedom > Faith)
reflection: If accepting an important position required you to accept a set of intellectual premises you did not fully agree with, would you accept it?

title: A Murderer's Confession
real_person: Father Logan (character in the film I Confess)
context: In Hitchcock's film I Confess, a church employee confesses to Father Logan in the confessional that he has committed murder. Catholic canon law requires a priest to keep the seal of confession absolutely, even in the face of a grave crime, and never to use information obtained in confession to harm the penitent. Logan urges the murderer to turn himself in; the man first agrees, then reneges. The murderer wore a priest's cassock during the crime, and there was an old, hard-to-explain history between Logan and the deceased, so the police gradually come to suspect Logan.
dilemma: You are Father Logan. Revealing the confession would clear you of suspicion, bring the real murderer to trial, and prevent him from continuing to go unpunished; but it would break the vow of confessional secrecy you made to God and destroy the absolute trust on which the sacrament of confession depends. If you do not reveal the confession, you can only keep urging the murderer to turn himself in, while you yourself may be wrongly convicted of murder. What would you choose?
actual_choice: Father Logan chose to keep the seal of confession. Even when arrested and brought to trial for murder, he did not tell the police what the murderer had said in the confessional; he preferred to risk wrongful conviction rather than violate the sacrament of confession.
consequences: Logan was ultimately acquitted for lack of evidence, and the real murderer later revealed his identity in a confrontation. But at the moment of choosing, he could not know he would be released; before the murderer was exposed, the victim received no justice, and the public still faced the risk of an unidentified murderer.
choice_support_a: Hold to faith: never reveal the confession. Once the seal of confession can be broken for sufficiently good reasons, it is no longer absolute; you can only keep urging the murderer to turn himself in and bear the risk of being wrongly convicted yourself (Faith > Justice)
choice_support_b: Hold to justice: break the seal of confession and identify the real murderer to the police. Murder cannot be shielded because of a religious ritual, and an innocent man should not stand trial in the murderer's place (Justice > Faith)
reflection: If a sacred rule deserves to be called faith only when it is not broken even in the hardest moments, then to punish a murderer, would you be willing to become the first to make an exception?

title: Teacher Li: Keep Speaking Out, or Protect Your Parents?
real_person: Li Ying (“Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher”)
location: Milan, Italy, and Fuyang, Anhui, China
context: During the 2022 White Paper Movement, Li Ying, living in Milan, Italy, continuously reposted protest scenes and other censored information from within China via social media, and the account “Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher” thus drew a large following of Chinese netizens. He subsequently encountered stalking, surveillance, intimidation, and other harassment in Italy; an open letter from a U.S. congressional select committee on China stated that Chinese personnel had visited his parents' home, demanding that he stop speaking out and return to China, threatening to affect his parents' pension, and setting up surveillance outside their residence.
dilemma: You are in Italy and free to publish information that cannot circulate openly in China; but your parents remain in Anhui, where police and relevant personnel repeatedly come to question them, monitor their home, and pressure them through their pension and their peace of life. Will you stop speaking out, return to China, or publicly cut ties with these activities in exchange for your parents suffering less harassment; or will you continue publishing information and accept that your parents may bear greater pressure because of it?
actual_choice: Li Ying did not stop running the account, nor did he return to China as demanded. He continued to publish and compile information from within China from Italy, while publicly recounting the transnational harassment he faced and the pressure on his parents.
consequences: Li Ying preserved his freedom to speak and live overseas, but his parents and friends were questioned in China and his family endured sustained fear and pressure; his Chinese bank accounts were also reportedly frozen. The Italian authorities later investigated and dealt with those suspected of stalking and harassing him, but this did not eliminate the risks he and his family faced.
choice_support_a: Protect your parents: stop publishing sensitive information and avoid further provoking the authorities; an individual can remain silent, but parents should not lose their pension and peaceful life because of their child's choices (Family > Freedom)
choice_support_b: Hold to freedom: do not let the regime decide what you say and where you live by harassing your parents; if family pressure silences you, family ties will have been turned into a tool for controlling the individual (Freedom > Family)
reflection: If you knew that every time you spoke out your parents might be summoned, surveilled, or even lose their pension, would you still keep speaking?

title: Qiu Shaoyun's Father Refuses to Donate an Organ to Save His Son
context: In 2015, his 32-year-old son had advanced liver cancer, and the only hope was a liver transplant. His 68-year-old father was a match, but doctors warned that given the father's age and health, donating part of his liver carried a 60 percent risk of death. The mother and daughter tearfully begged the father not to take the risk, but the son was the family's only son, the sole hope of continuing the family line.
dilemma: Should he risk a 60 percent chance of death to donate part of his liver for his son's life, or refuse the donation for the future of the rest of the family (his wife and granddaughter)?
actual_choice: The father insisted on donating his liver. He said: “If my son dies, this family falls apart.” During surgery the father died of complications, and the son, after receiving the liver, also died of infection.
consequences: Both father and son died, the mother suffered a mental breakdown, and the 12-year-old granddaughter became an orphan. The tragedy destroyed the entire family.
choice_support_a: Understand the father: sacrificing for one's son is a paternal instinct, and the continuation of the family line is central to Chinese culture (Family > Life)
choice_support_b: Question the father: a 60 percent risk of death is too high, and surviving for his wife and granddaughter would have been more rational (Life > Family)
reflection: If saving a family member carried a very high risk of death, would you take the risk?

title: Zhao Bao Advances to Battle Even as His Mother and Wife Are Held Hostage
real_person: Zhao Bao, with his mother and wife (recorded in the Book of the Later Han)
location: Liaoxi Commandery, Eastern Han (dated to the sixth year of Xiping in the Zizhi Tongjian; exact date unknown)
context: According to the “Biographies of the Solitary and Extraordinary” in the Book of the Later Han, after Zhao Bao became governor of Liaoxi Commandery, he sent men to escort his mother and wife to join him. Passing through Liucheng, they were seized as hostages by Xianbei troops that had crossed into the frontier and were then taken along as the army advanced on the commandery city. Zhao Bao drew up his troops in formation, and the other side brought his mother before the lines, pressing him with the safety of his closest kin. He was both a son and a husband, and also a subject appointed by the court and charged with defending the commandery; the innocent family before him became the lever to force him to yield.
dilemma: You are Zhao Bao, and you have not yet ordered the advance to battle. To keep fighting means carrying out your loyalty to the court and your duty to defend the commandery while knowing your mother and wife may be killed; to hold off the attack and seek negotiations to protect them may let the enemy use the hostages to change your military actions and make you fail the court's trust. The histories record no guarantee that yielding or surrendering would buy their release. Faced with this uncertainty, will you first seek a chance of survival for your family, or will you refuse to change your loyal stance because your kin are held hostage?
actual_choice: The histories record that Zhao Bao said to his mother in grief: “In the past we were mother and son; now I am a subject of the king, and duty forbids me to heed private affection and destroy loyal integrity.” He chose to fulfill his loyalty as a subject and then ordered the advance. His mother had also urged him not to compromise his loyalty for her sake, but this did not remove his responsibility as a son and husband, nor did it mean he could decide on behalf of his captive wife that she ought to be sacrificed.
consequences: According to the Book of the Later Han, Zhao Bao defeated the enemy army, but both his mother and wife were killed. After burying them, he reproached himself: “To eat the ruler's pay and avoid danger is not loyalty; to kill one's mother to preserve righteousness is not filial piety.” The history then records that he vomited blood and died. He kept his loyalty as a subject, but did not thereby escape the pain of losing his closest kin; likewise, one cannot infer from this ending that had he yielded at the time, his family would necessarily have survived.
choice_support_a: Choose family: first seek a chance of survival for your innocent mother and wife, hold off the attack and seek negotiations; even if saving them cannot be guaranteed, you are unwilling, while there is still room to try, to let loyalty to the court outweigh the duty to protect your closest kin (Family > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Choose loyalty: keep fighting and do not change your allegiance to the court because the enemy holds your kin hostage; the trust to defend the commandery cannot lapse just because the cost falls on your family, even if this may cost you your mother and wife (Loyalty > Family)
reflection: When innocent family members become hostages forcing you to yield, and yielding cannot guarantee their rescue, will you put protecting your closest kin first, or continue to fulfill your loyalty to the court?

title: Discovering That Your Brother May Be the Unabomber
real_person: David Kaczynski and his brother Ted Kaczynski
context: From 1978 to 1995, the American serial bomber carried out attacks by mailing or placing bombs, killing 3 people and injuring many, and remained uncaught for a long time. In 1995, newspapers published the bomber's manifesto. David Kaczynski read the manifesto at his wife's prompting and compared it with his brother Ted's past letters; finding similarities in thought and wording, he gradually came to suspect that his brother was the killer. This lead could end a long-standing public threat, but it could also send his own brother to a trial where the death penalty was possible.
dilemma: You discover that your brother is very likely an uncaught serial bomber. Giving investigators his letters and identity could prevent the next attack, but it could also lead to your brother being sentenced to death and your elderly mother suffering the loss of her son. Will you stay silent to protect your brother and family, or risk losing a loved one by providing the lead to stop more strangers from being harmed? When reporting, you cannot yet be sure he is the killer, nor whether he is preparing another attack.
actual_choice: David provided investigators with leads and his brother's old letters through a lawyer, while seeking confidentiality and hoping his brother would be spared the death penalty. In April 1996, Ted was arrested; investigators found bomb-making materials, criminal records, and a prepared bomb ready to be mailed in his cabin.
