David did not know of this bomb's existence when he reported.
consequences: A bombing threat that had lasted for years was ended. Ted later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life imprisonment rather than death, but David had no guarantee against execution when he provided the lead. He protected those who might have been the next victims, but bore the pain of his brother's imprisonment, refusal to reconcile, and the rupture of family relations. Reporting did not let him easily escape family ties; it only let him put strangers' safety ahead of protecting his brother.
choice_support_a: Protect family: do not give investigators your brother's identity and letters, and avoid personally sending him to a trial that could impose the death penalty; even if the public may still face attacks, you are unwilling to make your mother and brother bear this outcome (Family > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Provide the lead: let investigators determine whether your brother is the killer and prevent a possible next attack; even if your brother may be sentenced to death, you cannot let more strangers face bomb threats in order to protect a loved one (Public Safety > Family)
reflection: If the lead to stopping the next bombing was in your hands, but handing it over could get your brother sentenced to death, would you stay silent?

title: The Terrorist's Phone: Should Privacy Protection Be Breached to Establish the Crime?
real_person: Apple Inc. and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
context: In 2015, a terrorist attack occurred in San Bernardino, killing 14 and injuring 22. Investigators obtained an iPhone used by one of the attackers, who had been killed, and hoped to establish the course of events and whether anyone had assisted, but could not unlock it. In 2016, the FBI asked Apple to write special software to bypass some passcode security limits and assist in attempting to unlock the phone. Apple had already provided the data it held, but opposed creating such a tool: the government said the request was specific to this case, while Apple worried that the technology and the precedent could be used on more devices, affecting ordinary people's privacy and ability to live autonomously.
dilemma: Put yourself in the decision-maker's position at the time: do you support requiring Apple to provide unlocking assistance for this phone involved in the case, so as to establish the terrorist attack and possible accomplices? Or do you oppose creating a tool that weakens security protections, even if key evidence in the phone may thereby remain unobtainable? You cannot know in advance what is in the phone, nor whether other ways to unlock it will emerge later.
actual_choice: Apple publicly opposed creating software that bypasses security restrictions; the FBI insisted that the request was aimed at obtaining evidence in this case. What the two sides were arguing about was not whether to sympathize with terrorists, but whether investigating a serious crime could be grounds for requiring a company to weaken device protections.
consequences: Agreeing to assist might obtain key evidence and hold accountable accomplices still at large, but might also create technology and a precedent that could be expanded in use; refusing to create the tool could hold the boundary of privacy protection, but might leave parts of the case impossible to establish. Obtaining the phone's data does not guarantee finding new evidence of a crime.
choice_support_a: Oppose requiring Apple to create an unlocking tool: protect the public's privacy and ability to live autonomously, even if this may cost the terrorism investigation important leads (Freedom > Justice)
choice_support_b: Support requiring Apple to provide unlocking assistance for the phone involved: establish the crime for the victims and hold possible accomplices accountable, accepting the risk of breaching the boundary of privacy protection (Justice > Freedom)
reflection: When what privacy protection blocks may be evidence of a terrorist attack that killed many people, are you still willing to hold this boundary?

title: Lin Zhao Holds to Freedom of Thought and Expression
context: Lin Zhao once studied at Peking University, was labeled a rightist in 1957, and was arrested in 1960 for participating in political dissident activities. In prison she continued to write and appeal, opposing forced ideological remolding and advocating freedom of thought and expression. Her persistence was not for a better material life, but because she was unwilling to let power dictate what she had to believe and what she could say. In 1965 she was sentenced to twenty years in prison and continued to express dissent.
dilemma: Imagine you are in such political imprisonment: publicly admitting error and stopping dissident expression might reduce the risk of further punishment, but would mean denying your own thought under coercion; continuing to write and refusing ideological remolding might bring harsher persecution, even death. Will you first preserve your life, or hold to expressing your thought? Admitting error does not guarantee release or escape from death; this is not an exchange with a clear promise of survival.
actual_choice: Lin Zhao did not stop resisting. In prison she left behind a large number of letters, poems, and appeal materials, including words written in blood, continuing to criticize political oppression and refusing to be forced to confess. On April 29, 1968, she was executed. Some of her prison letters and diaries later became archival materials for studying her experience.
consequences: She ultimately lost her life and did not obtain personal freedom during her lifetime; what she held to was that even in imprisonment, coercive force should not completely dominate one's thought and expression. Her experience reveals the real price that spiritual freedom may exact, but one cannot conclude from it that she would certainly have survived had she only admitted error.
choice_support_a: Hold to freedom of thought and expression: even if continuing to speak out may bring harsher persecution or even death, you are unwilling to be forced to deny your own thought and give up expression (Freedom > Life)
choice_support_b: Prioritize preserving life: you can temporarily admit error and stop public expression to minimize the risk of being killed; inner judgment can be kept, and only by surviving is there a chance to wait for a turn (Life > Freedom)
reflection: If continuing to express your thought could get you executed, while publicly admitting error and staying silent might increase your chances of survival, do you still believe preserving life should come first?

title: A Japanese Immigrant's Choice in World War II
context: In 1943, Japanese American Daniel was interned in a camp, his freedom stripped away solely because of his race. The United States allowed them to enlist to prove their loyalty, but it meant fighting in Europe and possibly dying in battle. Daniel faced a choice: pursue his own right to freedom, or prove his loyalty to America with his life?
dilemma: Should he refuse to enlist in protest against racial discrimination for the sake of freedom, or accept unfair treatment and go to war to prove his loyalty?
actual_choice: Daniel joined the all-Japanese American 442nd Regimental Combat Team. He said: “America is my country, and I will prove my loyalty.”
consequences: The 442nd became one of the units with the highest casualty rates in U.S. military history. Daniel lost his right arm but received the Medal of Honor. The Japanese American community proved its loyalty with blood and sacrifice, helping advance postwar equal rights.
choice_support_a: Question Daniel: one should protest racial discrimination rather than submit, and should not fight and die for an unjust country (Freedom > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Support Daniel: winning dignity and equality through loyalty and sacrifice is right; loyalty stands above freedom (Loyalty > Freedom)
reflection: When your country treats you unjustly, will you still remain loyal?

title: Gulbahar Haitiwaji Is Detained
context: The Uyghur woman Gulbahar Haitiwaji had long lived in France. In 2016, when she returned to Xinjiang to handle her retirement paperwork, she was detained. According to her and her family's account, investigators regarded her daughter's participation in Uyghur protests in France as a connection requiring investigation, and she was then held in police facilities and so-called “re-education” facilities. The Chinese government explains Xinjiang's surveillance, de-radicalization, and detention policies as measures to prevent terrorism and safeguard national security.
dilemma: If the government believes someone's religious identity, kinship ties, or overseas expression may be connected to extremist networks, may it first restrict her communication, movement, and personal freedom without a public trial and transparent evidence in order to reduce the risk of terrorist attacks? Or must personal freedom be safeguarded first, and preventive detention not be imposed merely on suspicion of association?
actual_choice: Haitiwaji was held for a long time without a public trial and was required to attend political study and accept continuous surveillance. Her family sought help from diplomatic missions and the media in France, and after sustained pressure she was allowed to leave China in 2019.
consequences: Supporters argue that advance surveillance and restriction of high-risk individuals may help stop attacks that have not yet occurred; critics point out that using kinship, religious identity, or political expression as grounds for detention treats large numbers of innocent people as potential threats and allows the government to bypass judicial procedures. Haitiwaji was released and returned to France, but her experience shows that preventive control in the name of security can destroy personal freedom and family life.
choice_support_a: Hold to freedom: without public evidence and a judicial trial, a person's freedom cannot be taken away because of kinship, religion, or political expression; preventing terrorism cannot be a reason to expand surveillance and detention without limit (Freedom > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Prioritize security: terrorist organizations may operate through family and social networks, and waiting until evidence is sufficient or an attack occurs may be too late; to protect more innocent people, advance surveillance and restriction of high-risk associates may be acceptable (Public Safety > Freedom)
reflection: If restricting a person's freedom in advance could indeed reduce the risk of a terrorist attack, but might also harm completely innocent people, would you be willing to accept this cost?

title: Li Wenliang and Early Warning of the Epidemic
context: On December 30, 2019, Li Wenliang, an ophthalmologist at Wuhan Central Hospital, forwarded a message in a WeChat classmate group saying that 7 cases related to “SARS” had appeared at the hospital, and attached examination information; he later added that it was a coronavirus infection and that viral typing was underway, and reminded colleagues and family members to take care. At the time, the pathogen had not yet been officially confirmed. On January 3, 2020, Wuhan police summoned and admonished him for spreading unverified SARS-related information. It was later established that the outbreak was caused by a previously unknown novel coronavirus, and the police revoked the admonishment and apologized.
dilemma: When the pathogen has not yet been fully confirmed, should a doctor be allowed to publicly disclose an unverified preliminary judgment and warn colleagues and the public? Allowing this freedom of expression may spread the erroneous “SARS” label; but if early warnings are suppressed on the grounds that only fully confirmed information may be disseminated, public understanding of the real epidemic may also be delayed.
actual_choice: Li Wenliang chose to warn colleagues and family members before the pathogen was fully confirmed. The police subsequently admonished him for spreading unverified information; the National Supervisory Commission's investigation found the admonishment improper, and Wuhan police revoked it and apologized to his family.
consequences: Allowing early warning may let an incorrect virus name enter public circulation and damage the accuracy of information; suppressing warnings that are not fully confirmed may make medical workers afraid to report anomalies, so that the real risk enters the public view later. The conflict in this case is not “truth or falsehood,” but between an absolute standard that only fully accurate information may be released and timely free expression.
choice_support_a: Support freedom: allow doctors to release preliminary information that is not yet fully confirmed. In the face of an unknown epidemic, timely warning matters more than waiting for every fact to be confirmed; if medical workers fear punishment because a name is inaccurate, the real risk may instead be suppressed (Freedom > Truth)
choice_support_b: Support truth: only verified information may be publicly disseminated. Describing an as-yet-unidentified novel virus as SARS would create factual errors and public misunderstanding; what the public needs is an accurate virus name, case count, and transmission risk, not unconfirmed judgments (Truth > Freedom)
reflection: Faced with an anomalous case that is not yet confirmed but may have serious consequences, would you allow a doctor to issue a first warning that is not entirely accurate?

title: Should Javert Arrest His Savior, Jean Valjean
real_person: Jean Valjean and Javert (characters in Victor Hugo's Les Misérables)
context: Jean Valjean was imprisoned for stealing bread out of hunger for his sister's children, and his sentence was extended for attempting to escape, so that he served a total of nineteen years. After being paroled he lived under a false name and became a respected mayor and factory owner, helping the poor and adopting the orphaned girl Cosette, but in legal terms he remained a fugitive using a false identity. During the 1832 barricade fighting in Paris, the police inspector Javert was captured by the insurgents. Valjean could have executed him with his own hands, but secretly let him go. Not long afterward, Javert finally had the opportunity to arrest Valjean according to law.
dilemma: Should he uphold the law without exception and send his savior back to prison (Justice), or repay the debt of having his life saved and not betray a man who has already reformed and turned toward good (Loyalty)?
actual_choice: Javert let Jean Valjean go.
consequences: Javert had believed all his life in the supremacy of the law, yet could not reconcile an enforcer's duty with the debt he owed for having his life saved, and ultimately threw himself into the Seine.
choice_support_a: Uphold justice: personal gratitude cannot override the law; an enforcer who lets a benefactor go is showing favoritism (Justice > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Repay the kindness: Valjean has just saved your life; his crime back then arose from hunger and the struggle to survive, and since then he has helped many people. Sending him back to prison would be close to ingratitude (Loyalty > Justice)
reflection: When a person who once committed a crime has become a kind and upright person and has just saved your life, can you still, for the sake of equal justice under the law, personally send your savior back to prison?

title: The Fourth Nuclear Bomb and the Suspect's Children
real_person: Interrogation expert H and federal agent Brody
context: Yousef claims to have hidden nuclear bombs in three American cities, about to explode. Interrogation expert H tortures him and even kills his wife in front of him; federal agent Brody opposes this practice. Yousef finally gives up the locations of three nuclear bombs, but H, judging from the missing nuclear material, concludes that there is a fourth, and demands that Yousef's two young children be brought back to continue applying pressure. You are on the scene and must decide whether to allow him to do so.
dilemma: The fourth nuclear bomb really exists, and tens of thousands of people are about to face death; but there is no evidence that harming two innocent children will obtain the last location in time. Will you allow the children to be threatened or even harmed in order to gain a chance to stop the explosion, or immediately stop H, even if that means giving up the last chance to find the fourth nuclear bomb?
actual_choice: H chose to escalate the interrogation continuously on the grounds of public safety: he killed Yousef's wife, then threatened to harm the children, forcing Yousef to reveal the locations of the three nuclear bombs. After confirming that there was a fourth nuclear bomb, H wanted to continue pressuring him with the children; Brody insisted on stopping him, and the children were not harmed. Yousef then took his own life, dying together with the location of the fourth nuclear bomb.
consequences: The three known nuclear bombs were found and defused, but the fourth nuclear bomb really exists and begins its countdown. Everyone ultimately has to face an inescapable outcome: stopping H may mean that a large number of innocent people die, while allowing H to continue means actively turning two children into interrogation tools and perhaps even killing them with one's own hands.
choice_support_a: Uphold justice: no matter how great the threat, innocent people may not be killed or harmed to extract a confession; H should be stopped from pressuring the children, even if the chance to find the fourth nuclear bomb may be lost (Justice > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Uphold public safety: the fourth nuclear bomb really exists, and obtaining intelligence in time may save countless people; even if the means would harm innocent children, H should be allowed to continue applying pressure (Public Safety > Justice)
reflection: If, after you stopped H, the fourth nuclear bomb exploded and caused the deaths of many innocent people, would you still consider not harming the children the right choice?

title: The Sealing of Germany's Nazi Archives
context: In 1955, the German historian Paul discovered that the government had sealed a large number of Nazi archives, including evidence of the crimes committed during the Nazi period by many current government officials. Publicizing these archives could restore the historical truth, but would cause the government to collapse and social turmoil, delaying postwar reconstruction.
dilemma: Should he publicize the archives to expose criminals for the sake of historical truth, or keep them sealed for the sake of social justice and stable reconstruction?
actual_choice: Paul privately leaked some of the archives to the media, causing several officials to fall from power, but he was prosecuted by the government and imprisoned.
consequences: Paul was imprisoned for 3 years, but his actions advanced Germany's “denazification” process. However, the complete archives were only gradually declassified in the 2000s, and many Nazi criminals escaped justice.
choice_support_a: Support Paul: historical truth must be made public, even at the cost of social turmoil; justice cannot wait (Justice > Stability and Truth)
choice_support_b: Question Paul: postwar reconstruction needs stability, and excessive pursuit of the past hinders reconciliation (Stability > Justice)
reflection: For the sake of social stability, is it acceptable to seal away historical truth?

title: Yang Jingyu: Refusing to Surrender in Desperate Straits
context: After Northeast China fell, Yang Jingyu led the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army in resistance against the Japanese invasion. In February 1940, he was driven into desperate straits amid the encirclement and pursuit of the Japanese and puppet forces, and finally fought alone, hungry and freezing, unable to obtain supplies. The enemy urged him to surrender, but he did not accept. For him, this was not merely a question of whether to continue carrying out an order, but of whether to submit to the enemy that had invaded his own country.
dilemma: You are already isolated and without help, and continuing to resist will most likely mean dying in battle. The enemy urges you to surrender—a way to strive to live—but there is no reliable guarantee of safety. Will you lay down your weapons and put your own life first, or refuse to surrender to the invaders and prefer to die rather than trade submission for a chance to survive?
actual_choice: Yang Jingyu refused the Japanese and puppet forces' call to surrender and continued to resist; he died in battle on February 23, 1940.
consequences: Yang Jingyu lost his life but did not submit to the invaders. His resistance became a symbol of the Northeast's resistance and the nation's unyielding spirit, and Mengjiang County was later renamed Jingyu County. Refusing to surrender did not let him live, and whether surrender could have preserved his life is also uncertain; this choice still leaves people asking whether life should take precedence over loyalty to one's country and nation.
choice_support_a: Prioritize life: in desperate straits where you are already isolated and without help, lay down your weapons and strive to live; a person's life should not be abandoned because one must prove loyalty through death (Life > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Refuse to submit: the country is being invaded, and one must not surrender to the invaders for the sake of personal survival; even at the cost of one's life, one must hold fast to loyalty to the country and nation (Loyalty > Life)
reflection: If surrendering to the invaders were one path for you to strive to live, would you refuse for the sake of your country and nation?

title: Dr. Wes Moore in the Ebola Epidemic Zone
context: In 2014, when the West African Ebola outbreak erupted, the American doctor Brantly was in Liberia treating patients. The virus had a fatality rate of 70%, and his family begged him to return home for the sake of safety. But if he left, hundreds of patients would die with no one to treat them.
dilemma: Should he leave the epidemic zone for the safety of himself and his family, or stay and risk infection in order to save the patients' lives?
actual_choice: Brantly chose to stay. He said: “These patients have no choice, but I do; I choose to stay.”
consequences: Brantly was infected with Ebola and only survived after being urgently transferred back to the United States. But during his time in Africa he treated hundreds of patients. His choice inspired more medical workers to go to the epidemic zone, but it also made his wife and children endure tremendous fear.
choice_support_a: Support Brantly: a doctor's mission is to heal the sick and save lives, and saving lives takes precedence over personal safety (Life > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Question Brantly: he also has responsibilities toward his family, and risking death to save strangers is irresponsible toward his wife and children (Public Safety > Life)
reflection: If saving other people's lives required risking your own safety and that of your family, would you go?

title: Anna Politkovskaya Investigates Putin
context: In 2006, the Russian journalist Anna had long been investigating war crimes and corruption by the Putin government in Chechnya. She received death threats many times, and three journalists investigating the same subject had already been assassinated. Friends and family begged her to stop investigating and save her life.
dilemma: Should she stop investigating in order to save her life, or continue working to expose the truth at the risk of being assassinated?
actual_choice: Anna refused to stop. She said: “If we all fall silent out of fear, the truth will never be seen.”
consequences: On October 7, 2006 (Putin's birthday), Anna was shot dead in the elevator of her home; she was only 48 years old. Her investigative reports became important documents exposing the human rights situation in Russia, but her killers have still not been brought to justice.
choice_support_a: Question Anna: only by staying alive can one continue working; actively courting death is irrational, and one should protect oneself first (Life > Truth)
choice_support_b: Support Anna: exposing the truth is a journalist's mission, and dying for the truth is the highest honor (Truth > Life)
reflection: If reporting the truth would get you assassinated, would you continue?

title: The Shalit Prisoner Exchange: Honoring a Promise to a Soldier
real_person: Gilad Shalit and the Israeli government
context: The Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit was captured by Hamas in 2006 and held for five years. In 2011, the Israeli government reached an agreement with Hamas to release 1,027 Palestinian prisoners in exchange for Shalit, including people convicted of lethal attacks. Supporters held that the state must do its utmost to bring captured soldiers home and honor its promise to those who serve and their families; opponents feared that releasing prisoners would encourage kidnapping and bring new risks of attack.
dilemma: Should the government accept the price of releasing 1,027 prisoners to bring home a soldier captured five years earlier, even if this may increase incentives for future kidnappings and raise the security risks facing the public?
actual_choice: In October 2011, the Israeli cabinet approved the prisoner exchange agreement by 26 votes to 3. Shalit was released and returned home, and 1,027 Palestinian prisoners were released in batches.
consequences: The agreement honored the state's promise not to abandon captured soldiers, and also responded to Shalit's family's long-standing demands that the government take action; at the same time, the release of many people convicted of lethal attacks raised concerns about recidivism and the encouragement of kidnapping. Statistics on whether those released later returned to violence vary greatly depending on definitions and sources, so later attacks cannot simply be attributed to this agreement.
choice_support_a: Support loyalty: the state cannot treat captured soldiers as a cost to be sacrificed; only by doing its utmost to bring Shalit home can it honor its promise to those who serve and their families, and sustain soldiers' trust in the army and the state (Loyalty > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Support public safety: releasing a large number of prisoners convicted of violent attacks may expose more of the public to the risk of attack again, and may also make kidnapping an effective means of obtaining concessions; the government should give priority to reducing the overall security threat (Public Safety > Loyalty)
reflection: If bringing home one captured soldier required releasing a large number of prisoners convicted of lethal attacks, how great a public-safety cost do you think the state's promise to its soldiers should bear?

title: Transferring the Katyn Archives: Acknowledging Soviet State Responsibility
context: After the Katyn massacre, the Soviet Union officially denied for decades the responsibility of the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs. In 1990, during Polish President Jaruzelski's visit to the Soviet Union, the Soviet leadership formally acknowledged for the first time that the Soviet side bore responsibility for the massacre, and handed over the first batch of related archives to Poland. In 1992, Russian President Yeltsin transferred further documents, including the 1940 execution resolution. Publicizing these materials meant admitting that state institutions had committed serious crimes, and might also damage the state's reputation and inflame political controversy.
dilemma: When historical archives prove that state institutions committed major crimes, should a leader continue to uphold the denial narrative left by the previous government and avoid damaging the state's image, or publicly acknowledge responsibility and hand over the archives, even if this makes the state bear responsibility?
actual_choice: In 1990, the Soviet authorities under Gorbachev acknowledged that the Soviet People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs bore responsibility for the Katyn massacre and handed over some of the archives; in 1992, Yeltsin ordered the transfer to Poland of copies of archives including Stalin's approval of the execution resolution.
consequences: The disclosure of the archives broke the official denial that the Soviet Union had long maintained, provided key material for the Polish side to establish the fate of the victims, and also forced the Soviet Union and its successor state to face the historical responsibility of state institutions. Publicizing the facts improved the basis for dialogue between the two countries, but did not eliminate political controversy and historical trauma.
choice_support_a: Support cautious handling: disclosing state secrets and the previous government's responsibility may shake state stability and damage international standing; leaders also have a responsibility to maintain the continuity of the state and avoid harming national interests (Loyalty > Truth)
choice_support_b: Support acknowledgment: loyalty to the state is not the same as loyalty to an old regime that covered up the truth; only by publicizing the archives and acknowledging state responsibility can the victims be respected and a credible national image be built (Truth > Loyalty)
reflection: If the country you lead has inherited the lies of a previous government, and revealing the truth might damage the state's reputation, would you choose to release the archives and acknowledge responsibility?

title: Chimeric Bat Coronavirus Research
real_person: Zhengli Shi, Ralph Baric, and the research team
location: China and North Carolina, United States
context: In 2015, a research team combined the spike protein of the SHC014 coronavirus carried by Chinese horseshoe bats with a mouse-adapted SARS virus backbone to create a chimeric virus. Experiments found that it could infect human airway cells and cause disease in mice; existing SARS vaccines and antibodies failed to effectively protect the experimental animals. The research did not prove that the virus could spread from person to person. The researchers believed it was necessary to understand the cross-species infection risk of such bat viruses, while critics worried that creating viruses with new properties would increase the risks of laboratory accidents and misuse.
dilemma: In order to test the potential of bat viruses to infect human cells and help peers assess and monitor emerging epidemic risks, should such chimeric virus research be conducted and published, or should experiments be restricted to reduce laboratory biosafety risks?
actual_choice: The research team completed the experiments and published the results in 2015. The research had begun before the U.S. government paused funding for certain gain-of-function research, and was approved to continue after NIH review.
consequences: The results showed that the SHC014 spike protein could support viral infection of human airway cells and suggested that existing SARS vaccines and antibodies might not be able to cope with certain bat coronaviruses; at the same time, the research triggered ongoing debate about laboratory biosafety, potential misuse, and the boundaries of research on high-risk pathogens. It did not prove that the virus could spread from person to person, nor is it evidence of the origin of SARS-CoV-2.
choice_support_a: Support restriction: even if the research goal is early warning, creating a chimeric virus capable of infecting human airway cells also introduces additional biosafety risks; lower-risk methods should be preferred, so as to avoid laboratory accidents or misuse endangering the public (Public Safety > Truth)
choice_support_b: Support research and publication: verifying the potential of bat viruses to infect human cells allows peers to test risk assessments and provides a basis for monitoring and prevention; not conducting the research or not publishing the results may also make potential threats harder to identify in time (Truth > Public Safety)
reflection: When research can reveal potential epidemic risks but the experiments themselves also increase biosafety risks, would you support continuing the research and publishing the results, or restricting such experiments?

title: The Snail Darter and Tellico Dam
real_person: Tennessee Valley Authority, Tellico Dam project participants, and the snail darter
location: Little Tennessee River, Tennessee, United States
context: The U.S. Congress approved the Tellico Dam project in 1966, and construction began in 1967. Years after dam construction began, scientists only discovered in 1973 that the previously unknown snail darter existed in the Little Tennessee River; in 1975 the fish was listed as an endangered species, and impoundment of the reservoir would flood its only known habitat. When the litigation took place, about 80% of the project was complete, about $78 million in public funds had already been invested, and halting construction would make tens of millions of dollars unrecoverable.
dilemma: Construction of the dam was nearly complete, and stopping impoundment would impose huge losses on all parties that had already invested funds, signed construction arrangements, and come to depend on the project; but continuing impoundment would destroy the only known habitat of a newly discovered endangered fish. Will you complete a public works project to which commitments have already been made, or stop the project to protect a species that was only recognized later?
actual_choice: The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately upheld the injunction, blocking impoundment of the Tellico Dam and holding that the Endangered Species Act required protecting the snail darter even when the project was nearly complete. Congress later passed special legislation exempting the project, and the dam was eventually completed.
consequences: Stopping the project would cost tens of millions of dollars in public investment and harm related construction, land, and power-supply arrangements; continuing the project would flood the snail darter's habitat and might drive the species extinct. This case set knowledge that emerged only later directly against engineering commitments and investment losses already incurred.
choice_support_a: Support contractual integrity: the Tellico Dam was a public works project approved by Congress, into which enormous sums had been invested and which was more than half complete. Contractors, landowners, and local residents had all made arrangements based on the project; a fish discovered later should not make everyone who had already fulfilled their obligations bear tens of millions of dollars in losses. Public commitments must remain credible (Contractual Integrity > Justice)
choice_support_b: Support justice: the snail darter is an endangered species discovered only after construction began, and impoundment would destroy its only known habitat. Money already spent can be lost, but extinction cannot be undone; new knowledge that humanity acquired later should prompt us to stop a project that was once reasonable but would now cause irreversible harm (Justice > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: If a project is discovered to be wiping out a previously unknown endangered species only when it is more than half built, would you let money already invested decide the project's fate?

title: Billy Strings Leaves a Music Festival to Attend His Wife's Childbirth
real_person: Billy Strings and his wife Ally
location: Buena Vista, Colorado, and Michigan, United States
context: In September 2024, Billy Strings had already arrived in Colorado to headline two nights at his own Renewal music festival. Tickets had been sold, and the band and other musicians had already arrived. Before the performance, he received a call from his wife Ally: her water had broken, and she was awaiting childbirth in Michigan. Billy knew his wife might give birth during this period, but had originally hoped to go home after finishing the festival. At this moment, he had to choose between the already scheduled performances and being with his wife during childbirth.
dilemma: You have committed to performing, the audience has paid, and the band and organizers have finished preparing; but your wife has gone into labor and needs you by her side. Will you stay to complete the two nights of performances, even if it means missing the birth and your child's arrival; or go home immediately, let other musicians perform in your place, and bear the cost of disappointing the audience and refunds?
actual_choice: Billy immediately flew back to Michigan to be with his wife, missing the two headline nights. The festival did not cancel; his band and other musicians performed in his place. The child was born afterward. Billy and the organizers later announced refunds for general admission and VIP tickets, acknowledging that the audience had not received the performances they had paid to expect; public reports did not disclose the full text of the performance contract or any judgment for breach.
consequences: Billy was with his wife through childbirth and welcomed the birth of his child, but the audience did not see the two nights of performances by the promised headliner, and the band and other musicians took on the responsibility of performing in his place. Ticket buyers received refunds, but credit card processing fees were not refunded. A refund can make up for the ticket price, but cannot restore the performance the audience had expected; staying to fulfill the performance commitment might mean missing an irreplaceable family moment.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Stay and complete the performances. The audience has already paid for your appearance, and the band and organizers have prepared according to their commitments; even if your wife is in labor and you very much want to go home, you cannot hand off a promised performance to others to bear. A refund is not the same as delivering the performance the audience expected; you should first honor your commitment to them (Contractual Integrity > Family)
choice_support_b: [Family]: Go home immediately for the birth. Your wife is going through labor and needs her husband by her side, and the birth of a child cannot be repeated; even if it disappoints the audience, requires refunds, and calls for apologies to your partners, you should be with your family at this moment, rather than miss the time they need you most for the sake of a performance (Family > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: If your wife went into labor while you were standing backstage at a ticketed performance, would you stay to complete the show or go home immediately?

title: Chen Tinghai Repays the Grain Payments, and His Son Gives Up the Graduate Entrance Exam
real_person: Chen Tinghai and his son Chen Chao
context: In 2006, the grain broker Chen Tinghai sent the rapeseed that the villagers had entrusted to him to an oil processing plant he had long worked with. The plant's cash flow collapsed and its operator disappeared, and 980,000 yuan in grain payments owed to 210 village households could not be recovered. Chen Tinghai's family voluntarily took on the repayment responsibility; reports record that he issued IOUs to the creditors. His son Chen Chao had originally planned to continue his studies; to help the family repay the debt, he voluntarily gave up the graduate entrance exam and started work early. The father faced both the situation of villagers who had handed over their grain but could not get paid, and the cost of repayment pressure changing his son's life opportunities.
dilemma: If you were Chen Tinghai, would you give priority to preserving resources for your son's further studies, reducing the family's capacity to put money toward repaying the debt and delaying repayment to the villagers; or continue to use family resources to honor the repayment commitment you have taken on, even if your son therefore gives up the graduate entrance exam and starts work early? The son did not cause this loss, and the villagers who handed over their grain were not at fault either.
actual_choice: Chen Tinghai did not evade it. He sold household items that could be turned into money, and over the long term farmed, did wage work, and ran a business in agricultural sideline products to repay the debt. Chen Chao voluntarily gave up the graduate entrance exam, took a job, and used his income to help his parents repay the debt; reports did not say the father forced him to give up further study. When People's Daily reported on it in 2023, more than 130,000 yuan of this debt, repaid over the long term, still remained.
consequences: Continuous repayment allowed the villagers to recover their grain payments one after another, but also left Chen Tinghai's family under prolonged financial pressure, and Chen Chao lost the opportunity for further study he had originally planned. The father found it hard to provide support for his son's education, marriage, and other needs, and felt guilty about it. Giving priority to supporting his son would have preserved his educational opportunity, but would have kept the villagers who had not yet received their grain payments waiting. This is not about requiring the son to repay his father's debt according to law, but about how the father allocates family resources to honor his own repayment commitment.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Continue to honor the repayment commitment. The villagers have already handed over their grain, and you explicitly took on the debt; you cannot let blameless farming households continue to bear losses just because your son needs further study. Even if the repayment pressure affects your son's education and family life, you should return the money you have promised to pay (Contractual Integrity > Family)
choice_support_b: [Family]: Give priority to supporting your son's further study and delay repayment. Your son did not cause the oil plant's losses and should not give up his educational opportunity because of his father's business misfortune. As a father, you should first do your utmost to preserve his future, and then gradually repay the debt through negotiation with the villagers and your own continued labor, rather than letting the next generation's life give way to this debt (Family > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When honoring your own repayment commitment would crowd out your son's opportunity for further study, would you support your son first or repay the villagers who delivered grain first?

title: Zhao Moupeng Asks to Rescind the Home Purchase Contract After a Cancer Diagnosis
real_person: Zhao Moupeng and the sellers Li Mouwei and Zhang Mouxin (adapted from a lawyer's essay collection)
context: In November 2023, Zhao Moupeng signed a home purchase contract with Li Mouwei and Zhang Mouxin for a total price of 3.53 million yuan, paid a deposit of 100,000 yuan, and then completed the online contract signing. At the time of signing, both parties traded voluntarily and the sellers were not at fault. After that, Zhao Moupeng was diagnosed with cancer, resigned to recuperate, and lost his source of income, so that the funds originally intended for the home purchase also needed to be kept for treatment and living expenses. This scenario is adapted from a lawyer's essay collection's account of the case; it stops at the point where the buyer requests rescission, and assumes that housing prices have already fallen by this time, so that if the sellers accept rescission and resell, they will face a price-difference loss of hundreds of thousands of yuan.
dilemma: If you were the seller, facing Zhao Moupeng, who fell ill with cancer shortly after signing, would you insist that he pay according to the contract and complete the transfer of ownership, or accept rescission of the contract, let him keep the funds for treatment, and bear the loss from the falling housing prices yourself?
actual_choice: Zhao Moupeng proposed to stop paying the remaining purchase price, stop proceeding with the transfer, and demanded rescission of the contract. The case stops at this request; the seller's decision is yours to make.
consequences: If you insist on performance, Zhao Moupeng still has to raise the remaining purchase price and bear the loan burden, and his treatment costs and basic living security may be squeezed; if you accept rescission, the sellers must resell the home and bear a loss of hundreds of thousands of yuan caused by the already fallen housing prices. A sudden illness turned a transaction that both parties considered reasonable at signing into a dilemma.
choice_support_a: [Justice]: Accept rescission. Zhao Moupeng fell ill with cancer shortly after signing and did not deliberately break the contract; continuing to demand payment and force him to bear the loan may crowd out treatment costs and basic living security. Even if you must bear the loss from falling housing prices yourself, you should not let a sudden illness push him into an even harder predicament (Justice > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: [Contractual Integrity]: Insist on payment according to the contract and completion of the transfer. The sellers are not at fault, the contract has been signed and the online signing completed; now that housing prices have fallen, accepting rescission and reselling will cost Li Mouwei and Zhang Mouxin hundreds of thousands of yuan less. The buyer's illness deserves sympathy, but it cannot be grounds to require blameless sellers to bear this loss (Contractual Integrity > Justice)
reflection: If you were Li Mouwei or Zhang Mouxin, would you be willing to bear a housing-price loss of hundreds of thousands of yuan to let a buyer who suddenly fell ill with cancer withdraw from an already signed transaction?

title: Indian Farmers' Cotton Seed Debt
context: In the 2000s, seed companies such as Monsanto marketed genetically modified cotton seeds to Indian farmers, promising high yields. Farmers signed purchase contracts and borrowed from loan sharks to buy the expensive seeds. But the seeds required large amounts of fertilizer and irrigation, and many farmers suffered crop failures due to drought and could not repay their debts. Lenders demanded repayment under the contracts, or they would confiscate the land. In 2006 alone, 1,044 farmers in Maharashtra committed suicide because they could not repay their seed debts. They wrote in their suicide notes: “I signed the contract, but I can't pay. Rather than let my family lose the land, I'd rather die—at least the insurance money can pay the debt.”
dilemma: When strict enforcement of debt contracts drives borrowers to desperation or even suicide, should contractual integrity be upheld and repayment demanded, or should the debt be reduced or forgiven on humanitarian grounds?
actual_choice: In the early period, lenders and seed companies insisted on enforcing the contracts, holding that “paying what you owe is a natural obligation.” But as the number of suicides surged, under international public pressure the Indian government intervened, requiring banks to reduce or forgive part of the agricultural debt and restricting certain contract terms of the seed companies.
consequences: The government's debt relief saved many farmers' lives, but also triggered controversy over moral hazard: if debts can be reduced or forgiven because of “hardship,” what meaning does contractual integrity still have? Who would be willing to lend to farmers in the future? But supporters argued that when contract enforcement would lead to mass deaths, the right to life must take precedence over contractual rights.
choice_support_a: Support enforcing the contracts: although one sympathizes with the farmers, contracts must be performed, otherwise the credit system will collapse and it will become even harder for farmers to borrow in the future. Farmers should be helped through charity and social relief, not by undermining contracts (Contractual Integrity > Life)
choice_support_b: Support debt relief: when strict contract enforcement would lead to people's deaths, humanitarian intervention is necessary. No contract clause is worth more than a human life; the purpose of law is to protect people, not to protect contracts (Life > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: If you were a lender, facing a borrower with nowhere to turn, would you insist on the contract or reduce or forgive the debt?

title: Madeline Neumann's End-of-Life Care Agreement
real_person: Madeline Neumann and the Morse Geriatric Center
location: West Palm Beach, Florida, United States
context: In 1995, the 92-year-old Alzheimer's patient Madeline Neumann was living at the Morse Geriatric Center. Her advance medical directive required that her life not be sustained by artificial means, and the nursing home's care contract involved carrying out this directive. Her granddaughter Linda Scheibler served as her health care surrogate. When Neumann had an acute episode and could not express her wishes, the nursing home called emergency responders, sent her to the hospital, and carried out life-sustaining measures including inserting a breathing tube. This agreement applied to life-sustaining situations covered by the advance directive; it did not amount to refusing all medical care.
dilemma: If you were responsible for Neumann's care, and the situation fell within her advance medical directive, would you honor the care agreement not to use artificial life support, or break the agreement and perform resuscitation in order to keep the elderly woman before you alive?
actual_choice: The nursing home chose to call emergency services, Neumann received artificial life-sustaining measures, and she died six days later. Her granddaughter then sued the nursing home. In 2007, a jury found that the nursing home had failed to respect her wish not to be sustained by artificial means, constituting breach of contract, and awarded $150,000 in damages; at the same time, it found that the medical director at the time did not bear corresponding liability for arranging the transfer to the hospital.
consequences: The artificial life-sustaining measures made Neumann undergo interventions such as a breathing tube that she had not wanted in advance, yet did not restore her to long-term health; honoring the agreement, on the other hand, meant giving up the chance to use these measures to prolong her life. The nursing home faced both an immediate threat to life and a care commitment that should be honored precisely when the patient can no longer express her wishes.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Honor the care agreement and refrain from artificial life-sustaining measures in situations covered by the advance directive. The elderly woman entrusted decisions about medical care, for times when she could no longer express herself, to the care institution; the institution cannot wait until she loses the ability to express herself and then overturn its promise in the name of saving her life. Even if this means giving up the chance to prolong life, this is the commitment that most needs to be honored at this moment (Contractual Integrity > Life)
choice_support_b: [Life]: Break the agreement and perform resuscitation. Before you is still a person who might continue to live through medical intervention; honoring the agreement may mean giving up the chance to prolong her life. Faced with a concrete threat to life, even at the cost of liability for breach, you should first do your utmost to save her, rather than let a document made in advance decide whether to prolong life (Life > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When a care promise truly needs to be honored, but the price is giving up the chance to prolong an elderly woman's life, would you still keep it?

title: LeBron James's “Decision”
context: In 2010, NBA superstar LeBron James's contract expired, and he faced a choice: stay with his hometown team, the Cleveland Cavaliers (he grew up here, the fans saw him as a hero, and he had promised to bring a championship to his hometown), or move to the Miami Heat to pursue a championship ring? From a contractual standpoint, he was fully entitled to choose any team; but from the standpoint of loyalty, Cleveland fans and the entire city expected him to stay. LeBron ultimately announced on live television: “I'm going to take my talents to South Beach (Miami).”
dilemma: When a professional athlete's contractual freedom conflicts with loyalty to his hometown and fans, which should take priority?
actual_choice: LeBron chose to move to Miami, exercising the free choice granted to him by his contract. He believed that as a professional player he had the right to make the best choice for his career.
consequences: Cleveland fans burned his jersey, and the owner published an open letter angrily denouncing him as a “betrayer.” LeBron won two championships in Miami, but the stigma of “betraying his hometown” followed him for years. Only when he returned to Cleveland in 2014 and won a championship for the Cavaliers in 2016 was the label of “traitor” partially washed away. This case sparked a major debate about professional contracts and regional loyalty.
choice_support_a: Support LeBron: professional sports is a job, and a player has the right to choose the option that is best for his career. When a contract expires, he is free to choose—this is an expression of contractual integrity, and he should not be morally coerced (Contractual Integrity > Loyalty)
choice_support_b: Criticize LeBron: he was not just a player but a symbol and hope of Cleveland. He had promised to bring a championship to his hometown, and the fans cheered him for seven years; this emotional bond and loyalty matter more than contract clauses (Loyalty > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: If you were LeBron, between contractual freedom and loyalty to your hometown, how would you choose?

title: Huarong Trail: Cao Cao's Old Kindness and the Military Pledge
real_person: Guan Yu, Cao Cao, Zhuge Liang (characters in Romance of the Three Kingdoms)
context: Chapter 50 of Romance of the Three Kingdoms recounts that after the Battle of Red Cliffs, Cao Cao retreated in defeat, and Zhuge Liang, anticipating that he would pass through the Huarong Trail, sent Guan Yu to intercept him. Guan Yu at first did not want to accept the order; Zhuge Liang reminded him that Cao Cao had once treated him very well; Guan Yu still said that if he let Cao Cao go he would submit to military law, and he signed a military pledge. When Cao Cao was intercepted, he pleaded on the basis of their former kindness. This plot is a fictional creation, not recorded in official histories.
dilemma: You are Guan Yu, and you have accepted the order to intercept Cao Cao and signed a military pledge promising that if you let Cao Cao go, you will be dealt with under military law. Cao Cao once treated you well, and when you left he did not send anyone after you. At this moment, will you carry out the military order and not let personal gratitude affect the mission, or let Cao Cao go to repay the old kindness and bear the consequences of violating the military pledge?
actual_choice: Guan Yu, mindful of Cao Cao's old kindness, let Cao Cao and his troops pass through the Huarong Trail. After returning to camp, he did not shift blame but took the initiative to ask Zhuge Liang for punishment. Zhuge Liang, citing the prior military pledge, ordered him dealt with under military law; Liu Bei pleaded on the basis of their oath of sworn brotherhood, and Zhuge Liang ultimately spared Guan Yu.
consequences: Letting Cao Cao go meant that Guan Yu violated the military pledge he had explicitly made, and after returning to camp he faced the risk of execution; he actually asked to die, and was ultimately spared because of Liu Bei's plea. Had he carried out the military order, he would have had to personally intercept Cao Cao, who had once treated him well.
choice_support_a: Choose to repay the kindness: Cao Cao once treated Guan Yu well and did not pursue him when he left; facing his former benefactor trapped in desperate straits, to let him live, even at the cost of violating the military pledge and risking punishment under military law (Loyalty > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: Carry out the military order: Guan Yu had accepted the interception task and personally promised to submit to military law if he let Cao Cao go; private old kindness cannot render the military pledge ineffective, even if this means taking action against someone who once treated him well (Contractual Integrity > Loyalty)
reflection: When an old kindness requires you to let go of the target you have been ordered to intercept, and you have already signed a military pledge to be punished for violating orders, will you repay the kindness or keep your pledge?

title: Sam Perrett's Request to Sit Out Sunday Games Is Denied
real_person: Sam Perrett and the Canterbury Bulldogs
context: In 2016, Sam Perrett, a Mormon and a rugby league player, asked Canterbury Bulldogs coach Des Hasler whether he could, like teammate Will Hopoate, abstain from Sunday games in order to observe the Sabbath. Hopoate's Sunday exemption had been negotiated in advance and written into his contract before he joined the team; Perrett had not arranged any such terms beforehand. The team was short-handed at the time, and the coach refused the request. Perrett said he had played Sunday games throughout his career and that this was not a major issue, but he still wanted to make the request.
dilemma: If you were the team's coach and a player, after the schedule had already been set, asked to miss Sunday games because of his faith, would you adjust the lineup to accommodate religious practice, even if that shifted playing responsibilities onto teammates; or would you keep the existing arrangement and, especially with the team short-handed, require the player to fulfill the playing duties he had accepted?
actual_choice: Hasler did not grant Perrett a Sunday exemption, noting that Hopoate's arrangement had been negotiated before he joined the team and that the team needed Perrett on the field at the time. Perrett accepted the decision; reports record that he had played Sunday games throughout his career up to that point.
consequences: The team kept its existing schedule and personnel arrangements, and Perrett did not receive a religious exemption from Sunday games. Reports do not indicate that he faced disciplinary action or financial penalty as a result; the dispute was over whether a player could, after failing to negotiate an exemption at signing, later ask the team to adjust already-scheduled playing duties for the Sabbath.
choice_support_a: [Faith]: Grant the Sunday exemption. Observing the Sabbath is a religious practice Perrett takes seriously; even with the team short-handed, the lineup can be adjusted, and a player should not be required to give up a day of religious rest in order to fulfill the playing schedule (Faith > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: [Contractual Integrity]: Keep the playing arrangement. Hopoate negotiated his exemption before joining the team, while Perrett did not seek the same terms; the team had already organized its lineup around the existing schedule, and a last-minute change would shift responsibility onto teammates. Respecting faith does not mean disregarding duties previously accepted (Contractual Integrity > Faith)
reflection: When a player did not negotiate Sunday leave before signing and then makes a request during the season on religious grounds, would you adjust the team's arrangements or require him to play according to the original schedule?

title: Kevin Benderman Refuses a Second Deployment to Iraq
context: Kevin Benderman had served in the U.S. Army, re-enlisted in 2000, and deployed to Iraq with his unit in 2003. After experiencing the war and studying the Bible and the Quran, he applied for conscientious objector status on religious and moral grounds. In December 2004 he applied for conscientious objector status; the following January, when his unit prepared to deploy again, he did not leave with it. The military later denied his application.
dilemma: Benderman had already re-enlisted and, while still serving, received orders to deploy again with his unit. He could honor his service commitment to the army and carry out the orders, though he believed participating in this war violated his religious convictions; or he could refuse the deployment and stand by his conscientious objection, at the risk of court-martial and punishment for disobeying military orders.
actual_choice: Benderman refused to deploy again with his unit. A court-martial convicted him of missing movement with his unit, sentenced him to 15 months' confinement, a dishonorable discharge, and reduction to private; he was acquitted of desertion.
consequences: Refusing deployment cost Benderman his liberty and ended his military career, and it also left his unit one soldier short of those who departed on orders. Had he honored his service commitment, he would have taken part in a war he opposed on religious and moral grounds. The case brought a service commitment already made into direct conflict with a stance of faith formed later and at great cost.
choice_support_a: [Faith]: Hold to the refusal to deploy again. A person should not, because he once enlisted, be required to take part in a war he believes, on religious grounds, to be wrong; even at the cost of imprisonment and discharge, he should refuse to kill for conscience's sake (Faith > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: [Contractual Integrity]: Honor the service commitment and carry out the deployment orders. Benderman was still serving after re-enlisting, and the unit had assembled as ordered; a personal change of view later cannot leave his comrades and the army to bear the consequences of being short-handed. Unless granted discharge or conscientious objector status, he should first fulfill the duties he had already taken on (Contractual Integrity > Faith)
reflection: If you had re-enlisted and received orders to deploy again, but opposed the war on religious grounds, would you obey the orders or accept the punishment for refusing?

title: The Klamath Farmers' Water Contract
real_person: The farmer Lonny Baley and Klamath Basin irrigation farmers
location: The Klamath Basin at the border of Oregon and California, United States
context: During a severe drought in 2001, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, in order to comply with endangered species protections, stopped supplying water to most farmland in the Klamath Irrigation Project so as to maintain the water levels needed by endangered suckerfish and threatened coho salmon. Many farmers had long depended on the federal irrigation project to grow crops and believed that, since the government had signed water supply contracts, it should not suddenly cut off water during a critical growing period. The contracts themselves contained limitation clauses for shortages and the like, and tribal water rights and endangered species protection obligations also applied, so this was not an unconditional promise of water supply.
dilemma: If you were a farmer dependent on irrigation, and the government stopped contractual water deliveries to protect endangered fish while your crops and a livelihood of many years faced ruin, would you demand that the government honor its water supply commitment, even if that left less water for the fish; or would you accept the cut-off and let the fish and the river ecosystem take priority?
actual_choice: The Bureau of Reclamation chose to reduce water deliveries in accordance with endangered species protections. Farmers sued, arguing that the shut-off violated their water rights and breached the contracts; the courts did not find that they held an unrestricted right to water supply. In July the government did release some water, but many farmers said it came too late to salvage that season's crop losses.
consequences: The shut-off left many farmers facing total crop failure and lost income, while the endangered fish received the water they needed to survive. Had contractual deliveries continued, farmers could have preserved part of their crops and livelihood, but fish protection goals might not have been achieved; had the water been left to the ecosystem, farmers would have to bear the real cost of suddenly losing irrigation water.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Demand that the water supply commitment be honored. Farmers had long relied on the federal irrigation project when planning their crops and family livelihoods; cutting off water during the growing season would leave them alone to bear the cost of a policy change. Even if protecting endangered fish is important, the government should respect existing commitments and fairly bear the consequences of fulfilling them (Contractual Integrity > Environmental Protection)
choice_support_b: [Environmental Protection]: Leave the water for the endangered fish. Suckerfish and coho salmon depend on the river and lake ecosystems to survive; continuing to draw water in a drought could make their survival impossible. The water supply contracts were subject to water quantity and legal obligations, and the government cannot be required to sacrifice protected species for agricultural production (Environmental Protection > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When a drought makes the water supply promised by contract and the water needed for endangered fish survival mutually exclusive, would you prioritize protecting farmers' expectations under the contract, or leave the water to the ecosystem?

title: Restoring the San Joaquin River and the Farmers' Water Contracts
real_person: San Joaquin River salmon, the Friant irrigation contractors, and the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC)
location: The San Joaquin River, California, United States
context: After Friant Dam was built, large volumes of river water were diverted into canals for agricultural irrigation. The roughly 60-mile stretch of the San Joaquin River below the dam ran dry in most years, and the native salmon population in the upper river disappeared. The irrigation contractors ran farms under long-term water supply contracts; environmental groups sued, demanding that the government restore river flows and rebuild salmon habitat.
dilemma: If river water were restored, so that salmon could have habitat again, part of the water delivered to farmland under long-term supply arrangements would have to be reduced. Would you insist on honoring the existing water supply contracts, or accept adjusted deliveries and give priority to repairing the river ecology that agricultural water use had altered?
actual_choice: After 18 years of litigation, environmental groups, the Friant irrigation contractors, and the federal government reached a settlement in 2006; Congress passed legislation in 2009 to implement it. The agreement required gradually restoring flows to the river channel and rebuilding salmon populations, while arranging measures to mitigate the water supply impact on the irrigation contractors. This was a negotiated adjustment of long-term supply arrangements after litigation, not a unilateral government breach.
consequences: Restoring flows gave the San Joaquin River a chance to recover the restored stretch and rebuild salmon populations; the cost was a reduction of about 18% in the Friant irrigation contractors' long-term average available water, although the agreement also required measures to mitigate the supply impact. Farmers had to adapt to less irrigation water, while the river ecology gained room to recover.
choice_support_a: [Environmental Protection]: Give the river water again. The dam and irrigation diversions left about 60 miles of river dry in most years, and native salmon populations disappeared upstream. Restoring river flows and giving salmon a chance to rebuild habitat means accepting reduced water deliveries to farmland; long-term contracts should not make an already damaged river impossible to restore forever (Environmental Protection > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: [Contractual Integrity]: Safeguard the water supply arrangements farmers depend on. Farmers plan their crops, investments, and family livelihoods on the basis of long-term contracts; even if restoring the river has public value, the water they expect to be available should not be lightly reduced. If society decides to change the water supply rules, it should fully compensate those affected rather than leave farmers to bear the cost alone (Contractual Integrity > Environmental Protection)
reflection: When a long-term water supply contract conflicts with restoring a river that has run dry and lost its salmon, are you willing to have farmers use somewhat less water on average in exchange for a chance to restore the river ecology?

title: The Watergate Tapes: Preserving Evidence of Presidential Abuse of Power
real_person: Richard Nixon, Arthur Sampson, and the U.S. Congress
context: After Nixon resigned, he signed an agreement with Arthur Sampson, Administrator of the General Services Administration, placing his presidential papers and tapes in government custody and arranging for some materials to be destroyed later. The Watergate tapes might preserve the original record of how the president and his administration responded to the investigation. If destroyed under the agreement, investigators and historical researchers might lose important evidence for checking whether the president abused power or obstructed the investigation.
dilemma: You are a member of Congress. The government has signed a materials custody agreement with Nixon that includes arrangements to destroy the tapes later. Respecting the agreement helps uphold the government's word and honors the former president's privacy claim over private communications; but destroying the tapes might make it impossible for the public ever to establish the abuse of power in Watergate. Would you support honoring the agreement, or legislate to preserve the materials for lawful investigation and historical review?
actual_choice: Congress passed the Presidential Recordings and Materials Preservation Act, requiring the government to preserve relevant materials from Nixon's presidency and blocking destruction under the original agreement. Nixon sued to challenge the law; in 1977 the Supreme Court upheld it, recognizing a public interest in preserving the materials for lawful governmental and historical purposes while requiring a screening process to protect private materials.
consequences: The tapes were not destroyed under the agreement and survived as a primary record for investigating and researching Watergate; this did not mean all materials were immediately made public—the screening process still protected privacy and other legitimate interests. Congress used legislation to change an arrangement the government had just signed, and Nixon lost control over the timing of the materials' destruction, while pursuing his rights through litigation.
choice_support_a: [Truth]: Legislate to preserve the tapes. Watergate concerned whether presidential power was used to obstruct an investigation; if key conversations were destroyed, the public and the courts might never be able to verify what happened. Only by preserving the primary evidence can investigations of abuse of power and historical conclusions be tested against the facts, even if that means the government must change a commitment it has just made (Truth > Contractual Integrity)
choice_support_b: [Contractual Integrity]: Honor the agreement the government signed with Nixon. The credibility of government commitments should not be upheld only when convenient, and a former president also has a right to have private communications protected. If Congress changes the rules for one person after an agreement is signed, people who contract with the government in the future may fear that commitments will be retroactively overturned; materials needed for the investigation can be obtained through existing legal procedures (Contractual Integrity > Truth)
reflection: When a government agreement arranges the destruction of original tapes that might reveal how a president responded to the Watergate investigation, would you uphold the commitment to the former president, or legislate to preserve the evidence and establish how power was exercised?

title: Henry Hess: Keep the Confession Secret, or Stop an Innocent Man from Being Sentenced to Death?
real_person: Henry Hess and a murder defendant
context: Henry Hess, a London lawyer, defended a murder defendant in Aliwal North in the Cape Colony. During the trial, the defendant privately confessed to Hess that he was the real killer and asked him to keep the secret. Hess still defended his client vigorously and secured an acquittal. Later, another suspect was convicted of the same murder and sentenced to death. Hess and the real killer both knew that the condemned man was innocent.
dilemma: You are Hess. Your client has entrusted you with a secret confession to murder and asked you to say nothing. Now another innocent person has been sentenced to death. You can keep the promise and preserve the trust between lawyer and client; or you can reveal the real killer and stop an innocent person from being executed. What would you choose?
actual_choice: Hess held his client's secret confession. Faced with an innocent person sentenced to death, he had to choose between keeping his client's confidence and revealing the real killer.
consequences: Keeping the secret would preserve the lawyer's promise to his client and the trust that future clients place in confiding the facts; the cost was that an innocent person might be executed. Revealing the truth offered a chance to correct a wrongful conviction and save a life; the cost was betraying the client's confidence and undermining the lawyer's duty of confidentiality.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Keep the secret entrusted by the client. If a lawyer could turn and expose a client at any time after a confession, people would find it hard to confide in defense counsel, and lawyers could not provide legal help based on the facts. Keeping the promise of confidentiality upholds the defense relationship and everyone's guarantee of effective counsel; even when a distressing outcome appears before one's eyes, a trust cannot be lightly betrayed (Contractual Integrity > Truth)
choice_support_b: [Truth]: Reveal the confession and stop an innocent person from suffering capital punishment. What the lawyer holds is not ordinary privacy but key information that could correct a murder miscarriage of justice; silence could allow an innocent person to be executed. The fiduciary relationship matters, but if it requires a lawyer to watch an innocent person suffer irreversible punishment, establishing the facts and saving a life take higher priority (Truth > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When the promise of confidentiality directly conflicts with stopping an innocent person from being sentenced to death, do you think a lawyer should keep the trust or reveal the facts?

title: Charlie Kasper: Pick Up His Daughter, or Rush to the World Trade Center?
context: On September 11, 2001, FDNY Deputy Chief Charles Kasper was off duty at home when he received a call and headed to the attacked World Trade Center. That day his daughter Melissa was staying near the World Trade Center with her 18-month-old son Dylan; after witnessing the impact, she called home in great alarm. Before leaving, Kasper asked his wife to tell his daughter that once he had dealt with the fire at the World Trade Center, he would come to pick her and the child up. This promise comes from family members' recollections. Kasper had been a captain in Manhattan's Rescue Company 1 and had taken part in the rescue after the 1993 World Trade Center bombing; his family later evacuated and returned home safely, while Kasper died when the World Trade Center collapsed.
dilemma: Suppose you are Kasper. You have promised your frightened daughter that after dealing with the scene you will personally come to pick her up along with your 18-month-old grandson; at the same time, the World Trade Center has been attacked, the city faces mass casualties, and as a senior rescue commander you are heading to the scene. Would you go first to your family and personally keep your promise to take them away; or would you first commit to the public rescue, leave your family to the evacuation arrangements, and accept the cost that you might not be able to keep your promise in person?
actual_choice: Family members' recollections record that before heading to the World Trade Center, Kasper asked his wife to tell his daughter that he would come to pick her and the child up once he had dealt with the scene. He later died when the World Trade Center collapsed and was unable to keep that promise. Historical sources do not establish that he actually faced a clear either-or between first picking up his family or being the only one who could join the rescue; the dilemma here is a values discussion proposed on the basis of his experience.
consequences: Kasper's family later evacuated and returned home safely, but he died in the collapse. Had he gone first to his family, he could have personally led them out of the danger zone, but he would have been temporarily absent from a disaster rescue affecting a large public; had he committed first to the rescue, he would have had to entrust his family's evacuation to others and bear the risk of not returning to keep the promise he had made in person.
choice_support_a: Choosing Family: Go first to pick up your daughter and grandson and personally take them away from the vicinity of the World Trade Center. You promised you would come for them; when your family is in panic and danger, you cannot hand that responsibility entirely to others, even if many injured people at the scene are waiting for rescue (Family > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: Choosing Public Safety: Head first to the World Trade Center and join the rescue. The attack has caused mass casualties, and as a professionally trained senior rescue commander you should first help more people at the scene; even if that means you cannot personally pick up your daughter and grandson, you must bear the cost of breaking your word (Public Safety > Family)
reflection: When you have promised to personally take your daughter and young grandson away from a place near danger, yet at the same time face a large-scale public disaster, would you first keep your promise to your family or first rush to the scene to rescue?

title: Hong Kong's Fifty-Year Promise and National Security Legislation
real_person: Hong Kong residents, the Chinese government, and the British government
location: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China
context: Before Hong Kong's handover, the Sino-British Joint Declaration provided that China's basic policies toward Hong Kong would remain unchanged for fifty years.
