Deng Xiaoping, speaking about this arrangement in 1987, said the policy “would remain unchanged even after fifty years.” In 2019, the Hong Kong government proposed amendments to the Fugitive Offenders Ordinance on the grounds of closing legal loopholes in fugitive transfers; one of the triggers for the amendments was a Hong Kong resident who killed someone in Taiwan and returned to Hong Kong, while Hong Kong had no transfer arrangement with Taiwan. The amendments would have allowed suspects to be transferred to jurisdictions with which Hong Kong had not concluded long-term transfer arrangements, including mainland China. Many citizens believed the amendments would allow Beijing to expand its influence over Hong Kong's judicial affairs, breach the judicial autonomy and institutional boundaries Hong Kong had under “one country, two systems,” and therefore saw them as a dangerous step that changed existing arrangements and departed from a long-standing commitment; they held massive marches demanding withdrawal of the amendments. The initial large marches were predominantly peaceful demonstrations; in the months that followed, some assemblies turned into clashes between police and protesters, arson, and other violent incidents, and police use of force and mass arrests also occurred. The central government and the SAR government said Hong Kong faced a serious national security risk and that existing laws were insufficient to address it. In 2020, the NPC Standing Committee enacted the Hong Kong National Security Law and listed it in Annex III of the Basic Law, implementing it in Hong Kong.
dilemma: You are a decision-maker responsible for maintaining social order in Hong Kong. Facing continued street clashes and a national security threat as identified by the government, you can support stronger national security measures to reduce unrest and security risks; or you can uphold the long-term institutional commitment and require that all response measures must not substantively change Hong Kong's existing autonomy, rights, and freedoms. What would you choose?
actual_choice: The NPC Standing Committee enacted and implemented the Hong Kong National Security Law in Hong Kong. Afterwards, Hong Kong's Apple Daily ceased publication after police searches, the arrest of its executives, and the freezing of its assets; the 2021 electoral system reform reduced the directly elected seats in the Legislative Council from 35 to 20 and introduced candidate eligibility review; 47 democrats were charged with conspiracy to subvert state power for taking part in an unofficial primary, and 45 were convicted. In 2024, two former editors of Stand News were convicted of conspiracy to publish seditious publications; that case applied the sedition offense in the Crimes Ordinance, not the National Security Law.
consequences: Supporters argue that the national security legislation upheld national security and social stability; critics argue that these laws, enforcement actions, and changes to the electoral system have greatly narrowed the space for the media, political participation, and opposition activity, so that the autonomy and freedom protections of “one country, two systems” were substantially weakened before the promised period expired. The British government concluded that the National Security Law violated the Sino-British Joint Declaration; China denies breaching it, arguing that the Joint Declaration's transitional arrangements have been completed and that Britain has no right to interfere in Hong Kong affairs. The Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal continues to operate; whether judicial independence has “ended” is disputed, but the system of designated judges for national security cases and the resignation in 2022 of British Supreme Court justices from their posts as non-permanent judges of the Hong Kong Court of Final Appeal show that judicial independence is under significant question.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Hold to the promise of fifty years unchanged. Security risks need a response, but the government should still be bound by its public commitments and existing institutions, maintaining order through enforcement measures aimed at specific unlawful acts rather than using security as a pretext to substantially change guarantees of autonomy, elections, the press, and freedom of expression. If a commitment can be unilaterally reinterpreted whenever pressure arises, it will struggle to continue constraining power (Contractual Integrity > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: [Public Safety]: Give priority to strong national security measures. Large-scale clashes and national security risks may threaten social order and public safety, and the government has a responsibility to prevent the situation from deteriorating. Even if new laws and institutional reforms restrict some media activity, political organization, and freedoms, one may hold that safeguarding national security is the precondition for continuing to guarantee a stable life for the majority (Public Safety > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When the government believes national security and public order are under threat, and a forceful response would change the institutions and freedoms guaranteed by a long-term commitment, would you prioritize upholding the commitment or support the security measures?

title: Public Statements Before Shanghai's Lockdown and Public Trust
real_person: The Shanghai municipal government, the Shanghai police, and Shanghai residents
context: In March 2022, the number of locally transmitted COVID-19 infections in Shanghai rose rapidly. On March 15, a deputy secretary-general of the municipal government said at an epidemic briefing: “At present, we have not imposed a ‘lockdown,’ and there is no need for a ‘lockdown’ now,” adding that the city would carry out screening in key areas and grid-based management. On March 22, rumors circulated online that “Shanghai will be locked down for 7 days immediately” and the like; the next day police announced that two men had been placed under investigation on suspicion of fabricating and intentionally disseminating false information. On March 26, Wu Fan, a member of the city's epidemic prevention and control expert group, responded at a briefing that a lockdown was “not an option,” saying that Shanghai bears important economic functions. On the evening of March 27, Shanghai announced a phased lockdown divided by the Huangpu River, with Pudong and other areas beginning the next day and Puxi following. After the lockdown, residents encountered serious difficulties in the delivery of food and daily necessities, and officials acknowledged problems with the “last hundred meters” of delivery and took remedial measures. The police initially announced a criminal investigation, not a confirmed formal arrest or conviction; the earlier public statements were also not a literal “never lock down.”
dilemma: You are responsible for Shanghai's epidemic decisions. Infections are rising rapidly, and continuing only local screening without broader restrictions could increase transmission risk; but the government has just publicly said there is “no need for a lockdown now,” and the police have investigated people who spread news of a lockdown. You can pivot quickly to a citywide phased lockdown to reduce public health risks; or you can avoid abruptly overturning recent statements, giving priority to a credible explanation, advance warning, and preparation time, and preserving public trust in the government's commitments. What would you choose?
actual_choice: On the evening of March 27, Shanghai announced a phased lockdown: Pudong and related areas would begin controlled screening on March 28, with Puxi following. By then the number of infections had risen markedly, and officials explained the measures as a response to the spread of the epidemic and a way to protect public health; but this formed a sharp contrast with the earlier “no need for a lockdown now” and the March 26 public response that it was “not an option.” The police announcement of a criminal investigation into those spreading news of a lockdown further deepened the public's reliance on and confusion about official information.
consequences: After the lockdown, residents' movement and daily life were widely restricted, and insufficient delivery capacity made it hard for some residents to obtain food and other daily necessities in time; officials acknowledged difficulties in supply guarantees and last-mile delivery. Supporters of the lockdown argued that rapidly expanding controls helped reduce transmission and the risk of overwhelming the health system; critics argued that the government's repeated denials that a lockdown was imminent, followed by a sudden reversal, damaged public trust and cut short the time residents had to prepare. The scale and causes of the shortages were not single factors: extended lockdowns, insufficient delivery capacity, and constrained supply chains all contributed.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: The government recently stated clearly that there was “no need for a lockdown now” and responded to circulating lockdown news with a police criminal investigation. The public accordingly believed that a citywide lockdown would not be implemented soon and may not have stockpiled supplies or arranged care in time. Even if epidemic decisions need to be adjusted, the government should promptly and candidly explain changes in risk and give residents reasonable time to prepare; otherwise public commitments lose their binding force (Contractual Integrity > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: [Public Safety]: The number of infections rose rapidly in a short period, and continuing to rely on local screening could allow transmission to expand. The government has a responsibility to adjust strategy based on new epidemic data and adopt a phased lockdown to reduce public health risks; but it must at the same time clearly explain the policy reversal and ensure basic daily supplies and medical services (Public Safety > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When the government has recently said publicly that a lockdown is unnecessary and then, as infections rise, quickly implements a citywide phased lockdown, would you prioritize preserving public trust in the commitment and time to prepare, or support changing policy to control the epidemic?

title: The Yampi Sound Iron Ore Embargo: Honor the Supply Deal, or Stop Japan from Obtaining Strategic Resources?
real_person: The Australian government, Brasserts, and Japan's Nippon Mining
context: In 1935, the British company Brasserts and Japan's Nippon Mining arranged to develop the iron ore at Yampi Sound in Western Australia and supply the ore to Japan, with the Japanese side funding the project, and the Western Australian government had also approved the relevant leases. After Japan launched a full-scale invasion of China in 1937, Australia strengthened its defense preparations. In 1938, the federal government, citing geological reports indicating that economically recoverable iron ore reserves might be far lower than expected, announced a total ban on iron ore exports, blocking the Yampi project from supplying Japan as originally planned. A secret telegram from Prime Minister Joseph Lyons to the High Commissioner in Britain mentioned preserving the resources needed for domestic steel and defense, and also explicitly stated that he did not want firms associated with the Japanese government to establish a firm foothold in northwestern Australia. The Japanese investors protested and filed claims for losses. It should be noted that Australia's defense department had years earlier seen no obvious security obstacle to the project; the security necessity and government motives behind the 1938 embargo are therefore disputed, and there is no evidence that the Yampi project had become a Japanese military base.
dilemma: You are an Australian federal government decision-maker. The government had previously approved the development arrangement for the Yampi Sound iron ore in Western Australia, Japanese companies had invested funds, and the project planned to supply ore to Japan over the long term. Now Japan is at war with China and Australia is expanding its defense preparations; Australia's trade commissioner in Japan warns that Japanese capital could use the project to establish a strategic foothold in northwestern Australia, while geological reports say the country's recoverable iron ore reserves are limited. You can continue to honor the supply arrangement and uphold the approved investment and commercial commitments; or you can impose an export ban, preserve strategic resources and prevent a potential security foothold from forming, but bear investment losses, claims, and diplomatic conflict. What would you choose?
actual_choice: The Australian federal government announced a total ban on iron ore exports in 1938, effective in July of that year, and the Yampi project was therefore unable to supply Japan as originally planned. The government publicly explained the ban in terms of iron ore reserves and the needs of the domestic steel industry; Lyons's secret telegram also indicated that preventing firms associated with the Japanese government from gaining a firm foothold in northwestern Australia was one consideration. The Japanese side filed claims for investment losses, but available materials cannot prove that the project already constituted an imminent military threat; the defense department's earlier opinion had also supported continuing the project.
consequences: The embargo prevented Yampi iron ore from being exported under the agreed arrangement, set back Japanese investment and project development, prompted Japanese compensation demands, and put Australia-Japan relations under strain. Supporters of the embargo argued that iron ore was a strategic resource needed for defense and the steel industry, and that preventing Japan from expanding its economic influence in northwestern Australia could reduce future security risks; opponents argued that the government had changed a development arrangement it had previously permitted, made investors bear the cost of a policy shift, and that the defense threat at the time was not imminent and the resource shortage justification was also questioned.
choice_support_a: [Contractual Integrity]: Honor the already approved Yampi development and supply arrangement. Japanese companies invested funds on the basis of government permits, and commercial commitments should not be unilaterally overturned merely because political relations have worsened or because of speculation about future risks. If the government believes the project affects national defense, it can negotiate adjustments, provide lawful compensation, or present clear evidence, rather than leave investors alone to bear the losses of a policy change (Contractual Integrity > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: [Public Safety]: Impose the iron ore export ban, giving priority to preserving strategic resources and preventing Japanese influence from establishing a potential foothold in northwestern Australia. Japan has launched a war against China, Australia needs to secure steel raw materials for defense expansion, and it need not wait until a military threat is imminent to guard against strategic penetration. Even if the ban disrupts existing commercial arrangements and triggers claims, preventing national security risks can still take priority (Public Safety > Contractual Integrity)
reflection: When an existing ore supply arrangement involves strategic resources and the government fears that a potential enemy state could use investment to establish a foothold on its own soil, would you prioritize honoring the deal or take preventive embargo action?

title: Uyghur Recognition Alert: Security Warning, or Ethnic Profiling?
real_person: Test systems from Huawei and Megvii
location: China (the specific test site was not disclosed)
context: Internal Huawei test materials disclosed by a media investigation showed that a related video recognition system had been tested for ethnic recognition: when a Uyghur person was detected in the footage, the system would trigger an alert. That Huawei developed and tested such a feature shows it was not purely an abstract idea, and it has also raised concerns about its customers' needs and real-world uses. Huawei said the materials were for testing and denied developing surveillance products targeting a specific ethnic group; public materials cannot yet confirm whether a specific official order or large-scale deployment existed.
dilemma: You are responsible for product decisions at a technology company. A client wants to use a video recognition system to detect security risks faster; in testing, one feature can identify Uyghur identity and trigger alerts automatically. You can continue developing and offering this feature, believing it can help the relevant authorities respond to risks in time; or you can refuse to trigger alerts based on ethnic identity, avoiding treating a person's ethnicity as a danger signal and causing surveillance and differential treatment of an entire group. What would you decide?
actual_choice: In 2018, Huawei and Megvii cooperated in testing a video recognition feature that could identify ethnicity and trigger alerts. Public materials documented this test, but did not confirm whether the feature received a specific official order or was deployed at scale.
consequences: Triggering alerts based on ethnic identity could bring unrelated individuals into security screening solely because of their ethnicity, and could let ethnic labels replace concrete behavioral evidence. Huawei said the materials were for testing and denied developing surveillance products targeting a specific ethnic group; publicly available information is not yet sufficient to confirm whether the feature was put into actual deployment. The controversy over this feature highlights the risk, when developing recognition tools in the name of security, of treating individuals fairly and avoiding group-wide surveillance.
choice_support_a: Triggering alerts based on ethnic identity brings unrelated individuals into the scope of suspicion and may let ethnic labels replace concrete behavioral evidence. Even if the security goal is legitimate, measures should target specific risks and behaviors, not mark an entire ethnic group as a potential threat. (Justice > Public Safety)
choice_support_b: When the relevant authorities face real security pressure, video recognition and automatic alerts may help screen large volumes of footage quickly and improve the efficiency of detecting risks. Developers may believe that providing technical tools helps deal with potential dangers early and protect the public; but triggering alerts by ethnicity may also cause false alarms and unfair surveillance. (Public Safety > Justice)
reflection: Even if automatic recognition and alerts might improve the efficiency of security screening, do you accept a system that treats ethnic identity as a risk signal? How should security goals limit the uses of technology?

title: Zhang Zhan Documents the Wuhan Epidemic
context: In February 2020, Wuhan was locked down because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Zhang Zhan, a lawyer, traveled to Wuhan, visited hospitals and residential areas, filmed the scene, interviewed residents, and posted what she saw online. She kept documenting life and hardship during the epidemic so that more people could see voices from the ground beyond the official reports.
dilemma: Continuing to record and publish what you see with your own eyes might let more people understand the scene of the epidemic, but it might also bring prosecution by the authorities; stopping the filming and deleting the content could reduce the risk of being held accountable, but the situation of many people who lived through it might then go unknown. What would you do?
actual_choice: Zhang Zhan continued to post records of the scene of the Wuhan epidemic online. In May 2020 she was taken away by police; in December of that year a court sentenced her to four years in prison for “picking quarrels and provoking trouble.”
consequences: Zhang Zhan actually served four years and was released in May 2024 upon completing her sentence. She paid the price of losing four years of freedom for recording and publishing what she saw.
choice_support_a: Understanding the decision to stop: it is very hard for an individual to bear arrest and years of lost freedom. Deleting the videos and leaving Wuhan would at least preserve your personal liberty; recording the facts should not require a person to trade four years in prison for it (Freedom > Truth)
choice_support_b: Supporting the decision to keep recording: visiting in person, filming, and interviewing are important ways to keep the facts on the ground from being ignored. If everyone stays silent out of fear of punishment, the public will find it hard to learn what really happened in the crisis (Truth > Freedom)
reflection: If you saw suffering in a public crisis with your own eyes and recording and publishing it might cost you four years of freedom, would you still continue?

title: Cui Zhu Usurps the Throne, and the Grand Historian Writes the Truth at the Cost of His Life
real_person: The Grand Historian brothers of Qi and Nan Shi
context: In 548 BCE, Cui Zhu, a senior minister of Qi, killed the ruler Duke Zhuang of Qi, installed a new ruler, and took control of the government. The Grand Historian of Qi recorded state affairs on bamboo slips and wrote five characters: “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler.” Cui Zhu demanded that he change it; he refused and was killed. The Grand Historian's two younger brothers successively took up the brush, wrote the same words, and were successively killed. Now the Grand Historian's younger brother has once again taken up the brush.
dilemma: You know what it means to write “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler”: the three people who wrote these words before you are all dead, and the blade now hangs over your head. Write it, and you may become the fourth; change the ruler's death to a sudden illness, or simply leave it unrecorded, and you may survive. How would you write it?
actual_choice: The Grand Historian's younger brother still wrote “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler.” Seeing that he would not yield, Cui Zhu finally did not kill him. Nan Shi, hearing that the Grand Historians of Qi had been killed one after another, came carrying bamboo slips, ready to continue the record; only when he heard that the words had already been entered into the historical record did he turn back.
consequences: “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler” ultimately remained in the historical record, and the fact that the ruler had been killed by a minister was not erased. Three official historians lost their lives one after another for these five characters; the last person to write them survived, and Nan Shi, who came to continue the record, did not have to die. Later generations remembered the choices of these historians.
choice_support_a: Change it to stay alive: change “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler” to say the ruler died of a sudden illness, or simply leave it unrecorded. The first three historians already lost their lives for this; you need not be the fourth; a living person can still do other things (Life > Truth)
choice_support_b: Write it truthfully: write “Cui Zhu murdered his ruler.” A historian's duty is to record what happened exactly as it happened; if even historians alter the record out of fear, later generations will never know how the ruler died (Truth > Life)
reflection: If writing five characters truthfully could get you killed, while changing a few characters could save your life, how would you write it?
